stem: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Your agent needs to understand the dependency structure of a large codebase. What's the most efficient approach?

choices.text: Visualize the entire codebase first with external tools
Read every file in the codebase
Use Glob to find file patterns (imports, module declarations) and Grep to map relationships
Use Bash to run build tools or language-specific analysis (gradle, npm, cargo)

explanation: Glob finds files by name and Grep searches their contents, which is how the tools reference says to map a codebase without reading every file. Language-specific Bash (npm, cargo) can list declared dependencies, but it misses undeclared import edges and only works when that toolchain exists. Reading every file or an external visualizer blows the context window. Doc idea: Tools reference, Glob and Grep.

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.When the coordinator resumes an interrupted research session using session –resume, what must happen to ensure subagents have current information about changes in the research scope?

choices.text: Stale sessions cannot be resumed; always start fresh to avoid inconsistency
Subagents automatically re-read the coordinator's latest prompts and instructions
Use fork_session to branch from the previous session and let subagents discover changes
The coordinator must explicitly communicate any scope changes or new research directions to subagents in fresh invocations

explanation: Resuming sessions is efficient but requires explicit communication of changes. When you resume a coordinator session, the conversation history is preserved, but subagents are not automatically aware of new requirements. The next time the coordinator invokes a subagent, it must include: prior findings (from history), new research directions (explicit statement), and any refined criteria. This ensures subagents adapt to the evolved research scope Domain(s): Context Management & Reliability

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.Your coordinator implements a refinement loop: after evaluating findings, if gaps exist, re-invoke the subagent with specific gap prompts. How many re-invocation rounds should you allow before considering the research 'good enough'?

choices.text: Set a hard limit (e.g., max 3 rounds) to control costs and latency
Unlimited; iterate until the subagent reports completion
Re-invoke once per unique gap identified, then synthesize the result
Use adaptive stopping: continue if new information is discovered, stop when returns diminish

explanation: Implement adaptive stopping criteria in your refinement loop. Instead of fixed limits, evaluate whether each re-invocation produces new findings. If the subagent's second round returns mostly the same sources with confidence statements like 'exhaustive coverage of X', stop. This balances research quality with computational efficiency and prevents wasted iterations Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your agent encounters a large configuration file that the Bash 'head' tool would normally read in pieces. Should the agent use Read tool instead?

choices.text: Use Read only if the file is less than 100 lines
No; always use Bash for efficiency
No; large files should always be processed with Bash piping
Yes; the Read tool is better for reading file contents, especially large files, because it provides line numbering and handles formatting

explanation: Use Read for file exploration and content understanding. The Read tool provides line numbers, handles files transparently, and is designed for agent workflows. Use Bash for system tasks (running commands, piping output, scripting). This separation of concerns makes agent code cleaner: Read for 'I need to understand this file', Bash for 'I need to run this command' Domain(s): Tool Design & MCP Integration

choices.text: Skip it; old code is usually not important
Use Bash to count lines and estimate complexity
Use Grep to find test files or documentation that reference this module
Read the entire file to understand its full context

explanation: When exploring unfamiliar modules, tests and documentation are valuable resources. Use Grep to find test files (test_*.py, *_test.js, *Test.java) that import the module. Read the tests – they explain what the module does through usage examples. This is often faster and clearer than reading the module itself. Also search for comments or docstrings that reference this module Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

Search for(1) the function name to find declarations and references,(2) 'functionName(' to find direct calls,(3) imports of the module to find modules that might use it.Combine results to understand the full usage graph. stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent – You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. You're resuming a support session from yesterday using the --resume flag in the Claude SDK. The agent had gathered customer details and identified a billing dispute. What's the risk of resuming a stale session versus starting fresh with a summary?

choices.text: There's no meaningful difference; resume and fresh start produce identical agent behavior
Resuming is always faster and has no downsides compared to starting fresh
Resuming uses the old session's context window, potentially hitting limits faster if the conversation was long
Resuming guarantees the agent remembers the context, whereas a fresh session requires re-teaching the agent what happened

explanation: claude --resume restores the full transcript, including old tool results, so a long support thread consumes the context window again (sessions: what a resumed session restores). A summary-plus-fresh start drops stale turns. Resume is not free, and it does not 'guarantee' memory the fresh prompt cannot also state. Doc idea: Manage sessions.

stem: Scenario: You are building a multi agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates tasks to subagents (search, analyze, synthesize, report). When the coordinator agent calls a subagent using the Task tool, what is NOT automatically inherited by the subagent?

choices.text: Parent session context and conversation history
System prompt configuration
Tool definitions available to the agent
User authentication credentials

explanation: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context. It does not see the parent transcript, skills already invoked, or files already read (subagents: what loads at startup). It does get its own system prompt, a tools list, and project CLAUDE.md unless omitClaudeMd is set. Credentials are not the documented non-inheritance. Doc idea: Subagents, what loads at startup.

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. A scheduling agent uses one tool to retrieve available slots and another to book a slot. Many bookings fail because the slot becomes unavailable between those two calls. How should these tools be redesigned?

choices.text: Keep both tools and add retry instructions to the system prompt.
Combine them into a single find_and_book operation
Make book_appointment return richer failure details and alternative slots.
Add a hold_slot tool that temporarily reserves the slot between lookup and booking.

explanation: A slot that can vanish between lookup and book is a race. Combining the steps into one tool makes the operation atomic so the model cannot land between them. Retry text in the prompt does not reserve the slot. Richer errors and a hold tool help, but the smallest reliable fix for a two-call race is one operation. Doc idea: tool design for the agent loop (one tool, one effect).

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. How should you structure this decision-making?

choices.text: Queue all possible subagent invocations and execute in parallel regardless of relevance
Let the coordinator use model-driven reasoning to decide: based on the research question and available subagents, decide dynamically how to partition work
Create a decision tree in .claude/rules/ that lists all topic-to-subagent mappings
Hard-code rules in the coordinator's system prompt: 'Topic X always goes to subagent A'

explanation: Use model-driven reasoning for routing. The coordinator receives a research question, reasons about what subagents are best suited, and invokes them strategically. This is more flexible than hard-coded rules and adapts to novel questions. The coordinator's reasoning is transparent in its conversation history, making it easier to debug or refine orchestration logic Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

choices.text: Ask the user to manually edit the file
Use Bash sed to make the change instead
Use Read to examine the file, then use Write with a complete file rewrite
Try Edit again with a larger substring that includes more context

explanation: When old_string is not unique, the tools reference says to pass a longer string with surrounding context, or set replace_all. Rewriting the whole file with Write is how unrelated edits get dropped. Bash sed bypasses the Edit checks. Asking the user to edit by hand abandons the tool. Doc idea: Tools reference, Edit uniqueness.

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent – You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Your agent's system prompt includes a rule: "Always verify the customer identity before processing any refund." This is critical for compliance. You're concerned the agent might skip this step if it feels confident about identity from the conversation. What's the most reliable enforcement mechanism?

choices.text: Use tool_choice: 'required' to force the agent to always call get_customer first
Create a separate verification agent that must sign off before any refund can proceed
Implement a PostToolUse hook that inspects whether get_customer (identity verification) was called before allowing process_refund
Make the system prompt rule more detailed and explicit with multiple reminders about identity verification

explanation: PreToolUse can deny a tool before it runs (permissionDecision or exit code 2). PostToolUse fires only after the tool succeeded, so it cannot stop process_refund. tool_choice any or required forces some tool, not 'get_customer before refund'. A longer prompt is guidance, and permissions docs say CLAUDE.md does not enforce. A separate verifier that must sign off is the only listed design that can withhold the refund. Doc idea: Hooks, PreToolUse vs PostToolUse.

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Your coordinator detects that one research subagent is making repeated incorrect tool calls. What is the most reliable way to enforce compliance at the architecture level?

choices.text: Modify the subagent's system prompt to include stricter rules
Remove the misused tools from that subagent with its tools allowlist or disallowedTools. A query allowedTools list only auto-approves; it does not remove tools.
Use a PostToolUse hook to validate tool calls before they execute
Add a validation step in the coordinator that rejects bad requests

explanation: PostToolUse cannot validate a call before it executes. The subagents page restricts capability with the tools allowlist or disallowedTools. A stricter system prompt is not enforcement. Coordinator rejection after the fact is later than removing the bad tool. Doc idea: Subagents, available tools; Hooks, PreToolUse.

stem: Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. Your CLAUDE.md file is getting large and hard to manage. You want to split common standards into separate files while keeping the main CLAUDE.md concise. How do you reference these separate files?

choices.text: Create multiple CLAUDE.md files in different .claude/ subdirectories
Split the file manually and configure path matching in .claude/rules/
Use include: directives in the CLAUDE.md header
Use @import syntax to modularly reference other CLAUDE.md or configuration files

explanation: CLAUDE.md imports other files with @path/to/file. That is how you keep the main file short. The choice's '@import' wording is loose; the syntax is @path. Imports still load at launch, so they do not shrink context. Path-scoped .claude/rules/ load only when a matching file is read, which is a different feature. Doc idea: Memory, import additional files.

stem: Scenario: Multi Agent Research System — You are building a multi agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. When evaluating synthesis quality, the coordinator determines that key research gaps exist. What is the most efficient pattern for addressing gaps without restarting the entire research?

choices.text: Queue gap queries and execute all in a single new coordinator invocation
Invoke the search and analysis subagents again with targeted prompts to fill specific gaps
Use fork_session to branch from the current research state and explore alternatives in parallel
Summarize findings to date and start a fresh session with the new research direction

explanation: Subagents are meant to be invoked again with a narrow task message (common pattern: chain subagents). A fork inherits the whole conversation, which is the opposite of a small gap fill (subagents: fork the current conversation). Queuing everything in one coordinator call or starting over throws away the working split. Doc idea: Subagents, chain subagents.

Your agent is generating boilerplate code (a database migration script) and writes it to a file using the Write tool. After writing, what should the agent do?

choices.text: Run Bash to execute the generated code and verify it works
Read the file back to verify the generated content matches expectations
Ask the user to review the generated code before using it
Immediately return the file path to the user

explanation: After Write, Read the file back so the agent checks that the bytes on disk match the migration it intended. Running the migration can apply it for real. Handing the path to the user without a check skips verification the agent loop is built for. Doc idea: Agent loop, read after you write.

stem: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. An engineer who just joined the team asks the agent to help them understand the authentication and authorization architecture across a large multi service codebase. What exploration strategy most effectively builds understanding under context limits?

choices.text: Launch parallel subagents to explore different services simultaneously and then synthesize their findings.
Read CLAUDE.md and README files first, then ask the engineer to identify the most important files.
Read every file containing auth related keywords in content or filename.
Use Grep to find authentication entry points, read those files, and follow imports and function calls incrementally.

explanation: Grep finds the auth entry points; Read follows only those files and their calls. That stays inside the context budget (tools reference; keep context efficient). Parallel subagents are right for a broad sweep, but this question is one architecture the new engineer must understand in order. Reading every keyword hit, or stopping at README, either floods or starves the window. Doc idea: Tools reference, Grep then Read.

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Your agent's conversation history is growing long. After 10 turns, the context window is 70% full. You need to make a decision: continue the conversation or summarize and reset. What's the main reason to summarize and start fresh rather than continue?

choices.text: Summaries are always more accurate than full history
Continuing risks hitting context limits and losing the ability to make multiple tool calls or gather new information
Fresh sessions are always faster than continuing existing conversations
Summarizing automatically improves the agent's decision-making quality

explanation: Tool results accumulate. At 70% full, another multi-tool turn can hit the window before the refund is done (context window: what consumes context). A summary plus a fresh session keeps the facts and drops the raw history. Summaries are not more accurate than the history, and a fresh session is not automatically 'smarter'. Doc idea: Context window, compaction and clear.

stem: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude — You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. When your codebase exploration agent uses the Glob tool to find files, what is the primary value of Glob over using Bash find command?

choices.text: Glob is faster because it doesn't traverse directories
Glob can filter by file content, not just names
Glob works reliably across different operating systems with consistent pattern matching
Glob returns results sorted by modification time, making it easy to identify recently changed files

explanation: The tools reference states Glob results are sorted by modification time and capped at 100 files. That is the documented difference from a raw find. Glob does traverse directories, does not search file contents (that is Grep), and pattern portability is not the primary claim the page makes. Doc idea: Tools reference, Glob tool behavior.

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Your synthesis subagent needs to work from research conducted by both the web search and document analysis subagents. What is the recommended pattern for providing this information?

choices.text: Chain subagent calls: first get results, then invoke synthesis with those results passed as context
Pass the coordinator's summary of both subagents' findings in the Task tool call to the synthesis subagent
Have the synthesis subagent invoke both the web search and document analysis tools directly
Have each subagent store results in a shared database that the synthesis agent queries

explanation: A subagent only returns its final message to the parent. The parent then passes that text into the next Agent call (chain subagents). The synthesis agent does not see the others' transcripts and does not share a database. Giving it both tools collapses the split the coordinator is for. Passing only a coordinator summary also works, but the documented pattern is to pass the prior results as the next task message. Doc idea: Subagents, chain subagents.

stem: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. After a long exploration of a rendering subsystem, the agent starts responding with generic rendering patterns instead of the specific classes it had discovered. An engineer now asks how physics integrates with rendering for debug overlays. What is the most effective approach?

choices.text: Clear the context completely and restart the exploration from scratch.
Spawn a subagent to explore physics independently and manually synthesize later.
Summarize the key rendering findings, then spawn a subagent for physics exploration with that summary in its initial context.
Continue in the current context with more targeted prompts naming the specific classes.

explanation: When the main window starts inventing generic classes, the specific reads have been crowded out. Summarize the rendering facts, then spawn a subagent whose task includes that summary (context window: use subagents so raw reads stay out of the parent). Clearing everything discards the findings. Staying in the bloated window, or exploring physics with no rendering summary, repeats the failure. Doc idea: Context window, delegate large reads.

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. During a billing dispute resolution, your agent successfully retrieves customer info and order details, but when attempting to call process_refund, the tool returns a timeout error. The agent can explain the charges and verify refund eligibility, but cannot actually process the refund due to the backend failure. What approach best balances first contact resolution with appropriate error handling?

choices.text: Implement automatic retries with exponential backoff and keep the conversation open until the refund is successfully processed.
Escalate immediately to a human agent because the refund action cannot be completed.
Confirm the refund will be processed and close the conversation because the system has all necessary information.
Explain the billing, confirm refund eligibility, acknowledge the system issue preventing immediate processing, and offer escalation or retry later.

explanation: The agent already explained the bill and confirmed eligibility. The refund tool timed out, so it must not claim the refund was processed. Immediate escalation throws away a resolution that is otherwise ready. Infinite retries hold the customer. State the facts, the outage, and the choice to escalate or retry. Doc idea: tool results are data the agent must not contradict (agent loop).

explanation: Understanding the agentic loop is fundamental to agent architecture. The stop_reason field is a status indicator that tells you what the model wants to do next. When set to 'tool_use', the assistant message contains specific tool_use blocks with name and input properties. You extract these, execute them in your system (via MCP or direct function calls), and append the results back to the conversation history as a user message. This allows Claude to see the tool outcome and continue reasoning. The model-driven approach means Claude decides which tools to call and when, rather than following a pre-configured tree of decisions. choices.text: The subagent automatically inherits the parent agent's conversation history and tool access
The coordinator agent should block the subagent from calling any external tools to prevent conflicts
You must explicitly pass customer context and available tools to the subagent; context is not inherited automatically
The Task tool creates a new session, but both agents continue using the same conversation object

explanation: Hub-and-spoke architecture is valuable for complex agent systems where you want a coordinator to orchestrate work and delegate to specialists. The critical insight is that subagents have isolated context by design, which prevents issues like context explosion and unintended side effects. However, isolation means you must explicitly hand off information. When you invoke a subagent with the Task tool, you pass three things: the task description, the customer context (extracted from the parent's knowledge), and the allowedTools list. For example, a billing dispute subagent might have access to ["lookup_order", "process_refund", "escalate_to_human"] but not "get_customer" if you want to limit its scope. This explicit handoff protocol is what makes the architecture reliable and auditable Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

explanation: Escalation is a critical part of a 80%+ first-contact resolution strategy. A structured escalation protocol means the agent passes structured data instead of just a customer ID. When the agent calls this tool, it provides analysis that the human can immediately act on. This also makes escalations auditable; you can track why issues were escalated and whether the agent's recommendations were accurate. In practice, a well-designed escalation protocol reduces the actual escalation rate because humans see the agent's reasoning and can often resolve the issue faster than they could starting from scratch Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

explanation: Task decomposition is valuable when one conversation involves multiple independent problems. Instead of having a single agent juggle billing and returns logic, you spawn specialized subagents in parallel. The coordinator waits for all Task results to complete, then synthesizes a unified response. The advantage is specialization: a returns-focused subagent has tools and knowledge for returns, billing-focused subagent has tools for refunds and disputes. This reduces errors because each agent operates in its domain of expertise. However, this only works if the issues are truly independent. If the return affects a refund calculation, you need the agents to communicate or the coordinator to handle the dependency. In practice, for your customer support scenario, you'd decompose complex multi-issue requests and keep simple single-issue requests in the main agent for speed Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

Analyze all files together in one comprehensive review for consistency

This is a retryable scenario in 6 hours. How should you communicate this to the agent?

choices.text: Return a success result and let the agent figure out what happened
Return the error as-is from the backend without any transformation or categorization
Return an error result with isError: true, errorCategory: 'transient', isRetryable: true, and a human-readable message explaining the fraud hold and suggesting escalation
Immediately call escalate_to_human without telling the agent about the error details

explanation: Error handling in agents is about translating backend failures into actionable information. When process_refund fails, the raw error might say something like 'HTTP 400: account_locked_fraud_check'. That's not useful to the agent or to the customer. Instead, you normalize it into structured error metadata: isError (true/false), errorCategory (one of: transient, non_retryable, permission_denied, not_found, etc.), isRetryable (boolean), and details (human-readable explanation). For the fraud hold scenario, you return isRetryable: true because the agent can offer to call back in 6 hours, or it can escalate if the customer needs immediate resolution. This metadata gives the agent the context to make good decisions. In production, you'd implement error normalization in a helper function that maps backend error codes to your error schema, ensuring consistency across all tools Domain(s): Context Management & Reliability

choices.text: The agent can only call these four tools; any attempt to call tools outside this list will fail at runtime
The agent will attempt all possible operations but these four will have priority
The agent's system prompt is restricted, but it can request tools outside this list
Tool scoping is only a recommendation; the agent will ignore it if it seems necessary

explanation: Tool scoping is a fundamental security pattern in agent architecture. By defining allowedTools in the AgentDefinition, you're implementing role-based access control. Your main support agent should handle returns, refunds, and escalations, but it should not have access to create_account (that's for onboarding), update_customer_password (that's for account recovery), or suspend_account (that's for compliance). This scoping prevents accidental or malicious misuse. If an agent somehow becomes compromised or the prompt is adversarially modified, scoped tool access limits the damage. In a hub-and-spoke architecture, each subagent gets even tighter scoping: a returns-specialist subagent might only have access to ["lookup_order", "get_return_policy", "initiate_return"]. This narrow scoping makes each agent's behavior predictable and auditable Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration, Tool Design & MCP Integration

Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.You have a tool called get_customer that's critical for retrieving customer details. Your tool description currently says: 'Retrieves customer information.' A team member says this is sufficient. Why might this description be inadequate for reliable agent behavior?

choices.text: Tool descriptions should only be one sentence for brevity

The description is too vague. It doesn't specify what parameters are required, what output format to expect, what edge cases exist (e.g., customer not found), or when to use this tool vs. other alternatives
Detailed descriptions slow down the model's reasoning process
The description is fine; agents don't need detailed tool descriptions to use tools correctly

explanation: Tool descriptions are the interface between the agent and your system. The model relies on these descriptions to decide which tool to call, what input to provide, and what the output means. A vague description like 'Retrieves customer information' leaves too many questions: What if the customer doesn't exist? What fields are returned? Is this the same as lookup_order, or different? When a customer asks 'Is my order confirmed?', the agent might incorrectly call get_customer instead of lookup_order if the descriptions don't clearly distinguish them. A better description for get_customer is: 'Retrieves customer account details (name, email, account status, subscription info). Use this before refunds to verify active account. Input: customer_id. Returns: {id, name, email, status, subscription_active}. Returns error if customer_id not found.' This detail reduces ambiguity and improves decision-making. Include example queries and boundary explanations (e.g., 'Does not return order history; use lookup_order for that'). Well-written tool descriptions directly impact first-contact resolution rates Domain(s): Tool Design & MCP Integration

Your backend returns different failure modes: 'Insufficient funds in account', 'Account locked pending fraud review', and 'Refund window expired'. How should you structure the tool's error response?

Return success even on failure and embed error codes in the result for the agent to parse
Return all error messages as plain text strings without categorization
Throw exceptions and let the SDK handle error translation automatically

explanation: Error handling in MCP tools is about translating backend failures into actionable structured data. Your tool implementation should catch failures from the backend and wrap them in a standard error schema: {"isError": true, "errorCategory": , "isRetryable": , "details": }. The errorCategory field helps the agent understand the class of error (transient, non_retryable, permission_denied, not_found, validation_error). isRetryable tells the agent whether waiting and retrying makes sense. details provides a human-readable explanation and suggested next steps. For refund failures, you might have a helper function: def normalize_refund_error(backend_error) that maps backend-specific error messages to your standard schema. This makes error handling consistent and predictable across your agent Domain(s): Tool Design & MCP Integration

choices.text: Store tool definitions in a database and fetch them at runtime based on the project
Require each project to copy the full ~/.claude.json and edit it locally
Define all tools in ~/.claude.json and let each project's agent choose which ones to use via tool_choice
Define project-level .mcp.json files so each project can have scoped tool access independent of others

explanation: MCP server scoping is about managing tool availability across projects and environments. The two-level hierarchy (user-level ~/.claude.json and project-level .mcp.json) is intentional. Use ~/.claude.json for tools that are universally available (e.g., get_customer, generic logging). Use project-level .mcp.json to define or override tools for a specific project. For example, your billing support project's .mcp.json might specify a billing-specific MCP server, while your fulfillment project's .mcp.json specifies a fulfillment server. This separation has security benefits: a billing agent won't accidentally have access to fulfillment tools. It also has maintainability benefits: when you update the billing tools, you only modify the billing project's .mcp.json, not a global config Domain(s): Tool Design & MCP Integration

The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.You want the agent to dynamically decide which tool to call based on the situation. You're choosing between tool_choice: 'auto' and tool_choice: 'any'. What's the practical difference?

choices.text: any' is more restrictive and prevents the model from calling certain tools
auto' and 'any' are equivalent; both let the model choose any available tool
auto' prevents the model from using tools at all
auto' uses model heuristics to decide whether and when to call tools; 'any' forces the model to always call a tool in every response, even if it might not need one

explanation: tool_choice is a parameter that affects whether tool calling is optional or mandatory in a given request. With tool_choice: 'auto' (default), the model has three options: (1) respond directly without calling any tools, (2) call one tool if it thinks that will help, (3) call multiple tools in sequence. This flexibility is good for customer support where sometimes the agent can resolve an issue with existing knowledge. tool_choice: 'any' forces a tool call; the model must include at least one tool_use block in its response. This is useful for enforcing prerequisites. For example, if you set tool_choice: 'any' with allowedTools: ["get_customer"], you force identity verification before anything else. In your support agent, you'd typically use 'auto' for general interactions and then programmatically shift to 'any' at specific checkpoints (like before processing a refund). Note that 'any' doesn't let you specify a particular tool; it just says a tool must be called. To force a specific tool, you use tool_choice with the tool name directly Domain(s): Tool Design & MCP Integration

choices.text: Configuration should never be split across files; it violates best practices
Always add everything to the root CLAUDE.md to keep configuration centralized
Use @import to modularize the CLAUDE.md so different features (refunds, returns, warranty claims) are defined in separate files and imported as needed

explanation: CLAUDE.md uses a hierarchy and modularity design. At the user level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), you might define global principles. At the project level (project/CLAUDE.md), you import project-specific rules. At the directory level (project/src/CLAUDE.md), you import feature-specific rules. This hierarchy means you can have: (1) Global rules (apply everywhere), (2) Project rules (apply to this customer support project), (3) Feature rules (apply to the warranty handling module). When you add a new feature like warranty claims, you create .claude/rules/warranty-tools.md with tool definitions and constraints specific to warranty, then import it in the project CLAUDE.md. This keeps configuration organized and makes it easy to find and modify rules. The @import syntax is your primary tool for managing this hierarchy without duplication Domain(s): Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

Use real-time for all operations; Batch adds unnecessary complexity

explanation: Batches are for work that can wait, at 50% price, not for the live synthesis turn (Message Batches). Use them for the slow first research fan-out. They are not incompatible with tools, and they are not the right default for every coordinator call. Doc idea: Message Batches API.

Minimal comments; let the code speak for itself
Include extensive comments explaining every line
Use docstring format comments for all functions

explanation: Match the comments already in the repo, and add a line only where the decision is not obvious. Commenting every line and writing none are both worse. Docstrings on every function are a style the repo may not use. Doc idea: Memory, match project conventions in CLAUDE.md.

Automated code fixing and refactoring
Static analysis and pattern finding without modifying code
Performance optimization and algorithmic improvement

explanation: Read, Grep, and Glob do not edit files (tools reference: those calls are not writes). That set is a static review. It cannot generate docs by writing, cannot fix code, and cannot 'optimize' by editing. Doc idea: Tools reference, read-only tools.

Read the ORM model files (e.g., models.py, entities.ts) that define the schema
Use all three approaches to cross-reference

Implement a separate evidence validation tool that runs after synthesis
Include an optional evidence_notes field; subagents can skip it if they prefer
Add a required_evidence field that lists sources for each claim; validate programmatically that evidence exists

explanation: A required evidence list can be rejected when it is empty. An optional notes field is skipped (the trailing 'Correct' sentence in the old choice D was explanation text, not a fifth answer). 'Always cite' in the prompt is not a check. A later validation tool is extra; the schema is the contract. Doc idea: structured output, required fields.

Question: What's a key constraint you must understand about the Batch API in the context of agentic workflows?

choices.text: The Batch API can only process text, not JSON
The Batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request; each batch request is single-turn. You can't use the agentic loop inside a batch job
The Batch API is faster than real-time API calls
The Batch API supports full multi-turn agentic loops with tool calling

explanation: The Batches page says the worker runs the same server-side agentic loop as the Messages API, and that multi-turn messages and tool use can be batched. A result of pause_turn is continued with a follow-up request; requests are still processed independently. 'No loop inside a batch' is the claim the page rejects. Batches are not text-only and are not faster than the live API. Doc idea: Message Batches API, server tools and the agentic loop.

Batch API doesn't support multi-turn tool calling, so reviews must be stateless
Batch API can only be used during off-peak hours
Batch API limits the number of requests per batch

explanation: A batch is limited to 100,000 requests or 256 MB (batch limitations). That is the constraint for hundreds of reviews. The page also says tool use and multi-turn messages are supported, so reviews do not have to be 'stateless' for that reason. Off-peak and pre-approval are not limits on the API. stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Question: Your .claude/CLAUDE.md file contains system prompt rules for all coordinator and subagent definitions. How should you organize this to ensure subagents receive only role-relevant rules?

choices.text: Embed rules directly in each AgentDefinition system prompt to ensure isolation
Use @import to modularize rules; create separate CLAUDE.md files or rule segments for coordinator vs research vs synthesis subagents
Include all rules in a global section; subagents ignore irrelevant ones automatically
Define rules in .claude/rules/ with YAML paths that conditionally load based on agent role

explanation: Each subagent's markdown body is its system prompt, not the parent Claude Code prompt (subagents: write subagent files). Put coordinator rules in the coordinator prompt and research rules in the research prompt. @path imports load for the file that imports them at launch; they do not filter by agent. .claude/rules paths match file paths, not agent roles. A global prompt that agents 'ignore' is not isolation. Non-fork subagents also load project CLAUDE.md unless omitClaudeMd is set, so shared rules still arrive unless you omit them. Doc idea: Subagents, system prompt and tools.

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Question: Your coordinator session runs out of context midway through synthesis. What is the best recovery strategy?

choices.text: Increase the model's context window size
Export findings to a database, start a fresh session, and continue synthesis with the exported data as context
Prune the coordinator's conversation history to remove intermediate results, then continue
Resume the session with session --resume and continue from where it left off

explanation: --resume restores the full history (sessions). It does not free a full window. The context window page says the loop compacts automatically near the limit, and /clear or a new session plus a summary is how you continue with less. Increasing the window is not a user switch. Pruning by hand is what /compact does, which is not listed. Export the findings and start fresh is the listed recovery. Doc idea: Sessions and context window, compact versus resume.

stem: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Question: Your synthesis tool needs to produce output in a specific JSON format. Should you design it as a generic 'format_output' tool or a specialized 'generate_research_report' tool?

choices.text: Specialized 'generate_research_report' - it can be optimized for your specific research domain and output requirements
Create both; let the subagent choose
Implement it as an MCP resource rather than a tool
Generic 'format_output' - it can be reused across different scenarios

explanation: Design specialized tools optimized for specific tasks. A 'generate_research_report' tool with a JSON schema is clearer and more reliable than a generic 'format_output' tool. Specificity in tool design reduces misrouting and improves the model's ability to select the right tool. The schema enforces format compliance, and the description guides semantic quality Domain(s): Tool Design & MCP Integration

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: You're updating the agent to handle a new refund policy with complex conditions (different refund windows for different product categories, special handling for digital goods). This involves multiple files and rule changes. Should you use Claude Code's plan mode or direct execution?

choices.text: Use plan mode to review the multi-file changes, then execute the plan after approval, reducing risk of unintended side effects
Always use direct execution for speed, even for complex changes
Never use plan mode; it's too slow
Plan mode is only for documentation, not actual code changes

explanation: Claude Code has two execution modes: plan and direct. In plan mode (default in interactive sessions), Claude generates a plan and shows it to you before making changes. You can review, suggest modifications, and approve. This is valuable for complex multi-file changes where mistakes are costly. In direct execution (-p flag in CI mode), Claude makes changes immediately without review. You use direct mode for simple, obviously safe changes (adding a comment, fixing a typo) or in CI pipelines where review would be too slow. For your refund policy update, use plan mode: Claude drafts changes to multiple files (rules/refund-policy.md, agent.py policy logic, tests/test_refund.py), shows them to you, and you review before applying. This reduces the risk of bugs in financial logic Domain(s): Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your CI/CD pipeline uses Claude Code to auto-generate test cases for new customer support features. You want structured output (JSON format) and non-interactive execution. What flags and configurations should you use?

choices.text: Use --async to run in the background
Use -p for non-interactive mode, --output-format json, and --json-schema to define the expected JSON structure
Just run claude-code with the prompt and let it output text
You cannot use Claude Code in CI pipelines; it's only for interactive use

explanation: Claude Code is designed for use in CI/CD pipelines, not just interactive development. For automated code generation or test generation, you use the -p flag (non-interactive, don't prompt for approval), –output-format json to request structured output, and –json-schema to specify the format. Your CI pipeline might run: claude-code -p –output-format json –json-schema test-schema.json 'Generate test cases for the new returns workflow'. Claude generates test cases in JSON format, your pipeline parses the JSON, validates it, and stores it in your test database. This pattern is powerful for keeping tests in sync with code as the agent develops new features. The structured output ensures your automation can reliably parse and process Claude's output Domain(s): Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your agent's system prompt says: 'Process refunds quickly and efficiently.' But you find the agent sometimes refunds orders incorrectly. Why is this prompt guidance insufficient for reliability?

choices.text: Prompts cannot enforce rules; only code can
The prompt is fine; the agent just needs more training data

The prompt is vague and lacks explicit criteria. 'Correctly' means different things. You need specific rules like: 'Only refund if: (1) order is within 30 days, (2) customer status is active, (3) item is not digital media'
The agent understands the rule but is choosing to ignore it

explanation: Prompt engineering for reliability requires explicit criteria, not vague goals. Replace 'Process refunds correctly' with specific rules: 'Only process refunds if all of these are true: (1) Current date is within 30 days of order date, (2) Customer account_status is 'active', (3) Item is not digital media (no refunds for digital). If any condition fails, escalate with the failed condition in the message.' This explicitness helps the model understand the rules and make consistent decisions. However, explicit prompts alone aren't sufficient. You combine them with programmatic enforcement: a PostToolUse hook that validates these conditions before allowing process_refund to execute. If the order is outside the 30-day window, the hook returns an error: 'Refund denied: Order is 45 days old, exceeds 30-day window.' This combination (explicit criteria in prompt + programmatic validation in hooks) ensures reliability. Few-shot examples further reinforce the rules: show the agent an example of a correct refund (within window, active customer, physical item) and an incorrect refund (digital item, incorrect escalation) Domain(s): Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your system prompt describes the agent's goals but doesn't provide examples of how to handle ambiguous cases (e.g., 'What if a customer says they received the wrong item AND the return window expired?'). What's the benefit of adding few-shot examples to the prompt?

choices.text: Few-shot examples make the prompt longer but don't improve agent behavior
Only test data needs examples; system prompts don't
Few-shot examples show the agent how to handle ambiguous cases consistently, reducing interpretation variance and improving first-contact resolution
Examples should be in the conversation history, not in the system prompt

explanation: Few-shot examples in the system prompt are one of the highest-impact techniques for improving agent reliability. They work because the model learns patterns from concrete scenarios. For your customer support agent, include 2-3 examples of how to handle ambiguous cases: (1) 'Item received as described, but customer wants a refund for buyer's remorse' -> Offer alternatives (store credit, exchange). (2) 'Package was lost in shipping 60 days ago, customer just noticed' -> Verify proof, escalate for exception processing. (3) 'Billing dispute: customer claims they were charged twice' -> Verify transactions, offer immediate reversal if duplicate is confirmed. These examples teach the agent the decision patterns: sometimes refuse (clear policy), sometimes negotiate (leverage), sometimes escalate (edge case). Without examples, the agent might handle the same scenario differently each time. With examples, behavior is consistent. The examples also serve as documentation for your team: they show what the agent is expected to do in tricky situations Domain(s): Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: You want the agent to return escalation decisions in a specific JSON format with fields: issue_type, severity, reason_for_escalation, recommended_handler. You're concerned the agent might not follow this format consistently. How should you enforce structured output?

choices.text: Parse whatever the agent returns and convert it to JSON manually
Include the format in the system prompt and trust the agent to follow it
Structured output cannot be enforced; accept whatever format the agent produces
Use tool_use with a JSON schema. Define an escalate_decision tool that takes the structured fields and returns the JSON-formatted response, forcing schema compliance

explanation: Structured output is important for agent reliability and downstream processing. If you just ask the agent to return JSON, it might sometimes deviate (e.g., include extra fields, use different field names). To enforce structure, use tool_use with a JSON schema. Define a tool like escalate_decision that has structured input parameters matching your schema. When the agent calls this tool, the SDK validates that all required fields are provided and of the correct type. This guarantees that every escalation follows the schema. For your scenario, the agent would call: escalate_decision(issue_type='billing_dispute', severity='high', reason_for_escalation='Customer claims duplicate charge after 60 days', recommended_handler='billing_specialist'). The tool returns the escalation in the exact format you need. This approach also makes it easy to log escalations, route them to the right team, and track resolution rates Domain(s): Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your agent sometimes makes mistakes in refund decisions (e.g., offering a refund when the policy says the customer is ineligible). You implement a validation mechanism where, after the agent decides on a resolution, you check it against the policy rules. If the decision is invalid, you return an error and ask the agent to reconsider. What's this pattern called?

choices.text: Session pruning
Model fine-tuning
Retry-with-error-feedback, where the agent receives validation error details and has the opportunity to revise its decision
Tool result caching

explanation: Retry-with-error-feedback is a powerful pattern for improving agent reasoning without fine-tuning. When the agent makes a decision, you validate it against your rules (policies, constraints, precedent). If it violates a rule, you don't just block the decision; you return an error with a clear explanation of what went wrong and what the agent should try instead. For example, if the agent decides to offer a full refund for a damaged item that's outside the return window, you return: {"isError": true, "errorCategory": "policy_violation", "details": "Item is outside 30-day return window. Policy allows: (1) Exchange for new item, (2) Store credit at 75%, (3) Escalation to supervisor for exception. Which option fits best for this customer?"}. The agent receives the feedback, understands the options, and revises. Over many interactions, the agent learns the policy through examples. This is particularly effective in Batch API mode where cost is reduced, so you can afford more turns of feedback and revision Domain(s): Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your manager asks: 'Why can't the agent just review its own decisions to catch mistakes?' You explain that self-review has limitations. What's the primary reason self-review is less effective than independent review?

choices.text: Self-review cannot access the tool results
Self-review takes longer than independent review
Self-review is less cost-effective
The model tends to agree with its own previous reasoning even if flawed. An independent review instance (separate request to Claude) is better at catching errors the original request missed

explanation: Self-review is convenient but has a fundamental limitation: confirmation bias. When you ask the agent to review its own decision, it's prone to confirming its reasoning rather than finding flaws. In cognitive science, this is well-established. To get truly independent review, use separate model instances with different prompts and context. For your customer support scenario, the architecture might be: (1) Resolution agent: makes a decision (offer refund, escalate, suggest alternative), (2) Review agent: independent instance with a review-focused prompt that audits the decision against policy. The review agent doesn't see the resolution agent's reasoning; it just sees the decision and checks it against rules. If there's a conflict (e.g., resolution approved a refund outside the window, but policy forbids it), the review agent raises a flag. This two-instance approach improves decision quality without adding much latency or cost. For high-value customer cases, you can add a human-in-the-loop review gate as well Domain(s): Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your agent successfully resolves most customer issues, but sometimes it doesn't realize when it should escalate. For example, it attempted a refund for a case that required fraud verification. How would you improve escalation detection using prompt engineering and validation?

choices.text: Require manual approval for all refunds
Accept that the agent will occasionally miss escalation opportunities

Define explicit escalation criteria in the prompt: 'Escalate if: (1) Customer reports fraud or unauthorized transaction, (2) Multiple failed refund attempts, (3) Account shows suspicious activity.' Combine with a validation rule: Before process_refund, check if the case has fraud signals and block refund with escalation instruction
Tell the agent 'Always escalate for fraud cases' and hope it remembers

explanation: Escalation detection relies on two mechanisms: (1) the agent recognizing escalation criteria, (2) validation rules that catch escalation signals automatically. The prompt defines escalation triggers: fraud signals, repeated failures, high-value cases, etc. The validation rules (PreToolUse hooks) inspect every refund attempt and look for signals like: fraud keywords in the conversation, customer account risk scores, refund frequency patterns. If signals are detected, the rule escalates automatically, even if the agent didn't recognize the need. This defensive approach (prompt + validation) ensures escalation happens when it should. For your example, a PreToolUse rule might say: if process_refund is called AND conversation contains 'unauthorized' OR 'fraud' OR 'didn't order', escalate instead of refunding. This catches fraud cases the agent might miss while still allowing the agent to escalate when it recognizes the need (agent-driven escalation) Domain(s): Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your agent's conversation has grown to 8000 tokens. The customer has multiple unresolved issues, and the context window is nearly full. What's the best strategy to avoid hitting context limits while keeping the issues in scope?

choices.text: Force the agent to resolve all issues in the remaining context, even if it means skipping important steps
Summarize the issues (names, status, pending actions) in a concise summary (200 tokens), clear the history, and continue with the summary as context. Store the full history separately for audit
End the conversation immediately and tell the customer to contact support again
Ignore context warnings and keep the full history

explanation: Context management for long conversations requires proactive summarization, not passive hope. When you detect high context usage (>70%) with unresolved issues, summarize and reset. The key is that summarization is not lossy; it's a concise reformulation of the essential facts. For multi-issue conversations, summarize each issue's status, what's been decided, and what's pending. Example: 'Return: Initiated, customer provided proof of damage, waiting on return shipping. Billing: Investigating duplicate charge, will confirm by tomorrow.' This summary is a contract between the old context and the new context. The agent reads the summary and understands where you are without needing 20 turns of history. The full history is preserved separately (database, logs) for audit and compliance. This approach is standard in long-running customer support systems and enables agents to handle conversations of any length without hitting context limits Domain(s): Context Management & Reliability

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your agent calls lookup_order and receives a response with 50 fields (order ID, customer ID, items, payment method, shipping address, billing address, dates, statuses, tracking info, notes, metadata, etc.). You want to include this in the conversation history to keep context efficient. What should you do with the tool result?

choices.text: Include the entire 50-field response as-is in the conversation history
Compress the result to a base64 string and include in history
Prune the result to relevant fields only (e.g., order ID, items, status, tracking) and include the pruned version in history. This keeps context efficient while preserving necessary information
Don't include tool results in the conversation history at all

explanation: Tool result pruning is essential for context efficiency in agent systems. When a tool returns rich data, you don't include it all. You extract the fields relevant to the current task and append only those to the conversation history. This is a common pattern in enterprise systems. For example, get_customer might return {id, name, email, phone, account_status, subscription_details, payment_methods, addresses, preferences, order_count, lifetime_value, notes, risk_score, created_date}. If the agent is verifying account status for a refund, you only need {id, account_status}. If the agent is looking up contact info for outreach, you need {name, email, phone}. You make the pruning decision based on the agent's task. In practice, you implement a pruning function for each tool: def prune_order_result(result, context_type) that returns only the relevant fields based on whether the context is 'tracking', 'billing', 'return', etc. This makes the agent more efficient and reduces context bloat Domain(s): Context Management & Reliability

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your support agent handles multiple concurrent customer issues in a single conversation. One issue is resolved (return approved), but the other (billing dispute) needs more investigation. How should you track state across multiple issues to avoid losing context?

choices.text: Just keep chatting; the agent will remember all issues
Have the agent tell the customer which issues are resolved

Implement structured state tracking: maintain a record of each issue's status, decisions made, and next steps. Include this state in the context explicitly as the conversation progresses (e.g., 'OPEN ISSUES: Return (approved, return label sent), Billing (investigating, will follow up tomorrow')
Create a new session for each issue

explanation: Multi-issue conversations require structured state tracking. Instead of relying on the agent to remember all issues, you explicitly track state and include it in the context. This is similar to how a human support representative would maintain a case file with sections like 'Issues Addressed', 'Decisions Made', 'Pending Actions'. For your customer support agent, implement a state block that updates after each significant interaction: a customer has a return and a billing issue. After handling the return, state is updated: 'Return (approved, label sent)'. After investigating billing, state is updated: 'Billing (duplicate charge confirmed, refund of $50 queued)'. The agent references this state to understand what's resolved and what's pending, reducing the risk of repeating work or losing context. For very long conversations (20+ turns with multiple issues), this state tracking becomes the anchor that keeps the conversation coherent Domain(s): Context Management & Reliability

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: Your agent encounters a situation where get_customer returns an error: 'Customer not found.' But the customer ID provided was what the user gave you. Is this a transient error or a non-retryable error? What should the agent do?

choices.text: It's a server error; scale up capacity
Ignore the error and return a dummy customer object

It's non-retryable. The customer ID doesn't exist in your system. Return {"isError": true, "errorCategory": "not_found", "isRetryable": false} and instruct the agent to ask the customer for verification (perhaps they misremembered their ID, or it's a new customer not yet in the system)
It's transient; retry immediately

explanation: Error categorization is crucial for agent decision-making. You need to distinguish between: (1) Transient errors (database timeout, network glitch) -> retry, (2) Non-retryable errors (customer not found, invalid input, permission denied) -> escalate or adapt, (3) Server errors (500, overloaded) -> retry with backoff. For 'Customer not found', the error is permanent for that ID. Retrying won't help. The agent should ask the customer for clarification: 'I couldn't find your account with that ID. Could you provide your email address or phone number instead?' This is a common pattern in support conversations. New customers might not have an ID yet; established customers might have forgotten their ID format. By properly categorizing the error and providing the agent with context, you enable graceful recovery instead of a dead-end Domain(s): Context Management & Reliability

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: You decide to start a fresh session for a resumed conversation the next day instead of using –resume. You summarize the previous session and pass it as context. What's the benefit of this approach over resuming the old session?

choices.text: Fresh sessions are cheaper
There's no real difference between resume and fresh sessions

A fresh session with a summary starts with 20-30% context usage instead of 70%+ from the old session. This preserves context window for new work and can improve reasoning clarity by focusing on essential facts vs. full history
Fresh sessions are always faster

explanation: The choice between resuming and fresh sessions depends on conversation length and staleness. For short, recent conversations (same day, under 3000 tokens), resuming preserves continuity and is efficient. For long or stale conversations, a fresh session with a summary is better. The summary should be a concise factual record: 'Customer Jane (ID: 12345) initiated a return for order 789. Return approved, customer will ship item back. Customer also has billing dispute for $50 charge. Investigating duplicate charge, will confirm tomorrow.' This summary (maybe 60 tokens) gives the agent a clear understanding without loading the full history. The agent has 7800+ tokens of context available for today's work. In production customer support systems, this hybrid approach (summarize + restart) is standard for conversations spanning multiple days or touchpoints Domain(s): Context Management & Reliability

This adaptability is a strength of agentic systems Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

stem: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: You want to ensure the agent always checks the refund policy before calling process_refund. You're considering two approaches: (1) Include the policy in the system prompt, (2) Implement a PreToolUse hook that validates the policy. Why is approach 2 more reliable?

choices.text: System prompts are sufficient; hooks are unnecessary overhead
PreToolUse hooks are faster than system prompts
Only one approach can be used at a time
PreToolUse hooks provide programmatic enforcement that's independent of the model's reasoning. If the policy is in the system prompt and the model forgets or rationalizes, the hook still catches it

explanation: Reliability in agent systems comes from layered enforcement, not just guidance. A system prompt rule ('Check the 30-day refund window before processing refunds') is helpful for steering the model, but it's not foolproof. Under pressure or when rationalizing, the model might skip the check. A PreToolUse hook provides a hard enforcement layer: before process_refund executes, the hook inspects the order date from the conversation history. If the order is outside the window, the hook returns an error with details. This blocks the refund and tells the agent why. The ideal architecture uses both: (1) System prompt with explicit policy, (2) PreToolUse hook for validation. The prompt guides the model; the hook enforces. This combination is why agents with hook-based enforcement achieve higher reliability than agents relying on prompts alone Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration, Tool Design & MCP Integration

It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Question: After a customer escalation is sent to the human team, you want to track what the human did and ensure the agent learns from it. What's a good pattern for closing the loop and improving the agent?

choices.text: Implement a feedback loop: after human resolution, record the decision (approved refund, negotiated discount, etc.) and the reasoning. Use this to refine the agent's future behavior (improve system prompt, add examples, adjust policies)
Agent behavior can't be improved; accept that escalations are permanent
Have the human agent document their action separately; the support agent doesn't need to know
Only collect feedback for failed escalations, not successful ones

explanation: Closing the feedback loop from escalations is how agents improve. After a human handles an escalated case, you analyze the decision: Did the human approve or deny? What was the reasoning? Did they apply an exception? Was there a policy interpretation? This data feeds back into agent improvement. If human agents frequently approve exceptions for product defects, your agent's system prompt should be updated to mention that possibility. If humans often negotiate discounts instead of offering refunds, your agent should learn to suggest discounts. This feedback loop transforms escalations from failures into learning data. In ML terminology, escalations are supervised examples where a human corrected the agent's decision. Over time, with good feedback mechanisms, your escalation rate should decrease as the agent learns from human patterns. This is how you move from 80% first-contact resolution (typical for new agents) to 90%+ (agents that have learned from lots of feedback) Domain(s): Agentic Architecture & Orchestration, Tool Design & MCP Integration

A colleague argues that tool descriptions should be minimal to 'keep things simple.' What's your response?

choices.text: Tool descriptions should be minimal; detailed descriptions confuse the model
Tool descriptions are just metadata; they don't affect agent behavior

Detailed tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for LLM tool selection. Vague descriptions lead to wrong tool choices and failed attempts. Include input formats, output examples, edge cases, and when NOT to use the tool
Tool descriptions should only describe inputs, not outputs

explanation: Tool descriptions are not boilerplate; they're critical for agent reliability. Detailed descriptions do three things: (1) Help the model decide when to use the tool, (2) Clarify what inputs are required and in what format, (3) Explain what to expect in the output and what errors might occur. A vague description like 'Gets order information' forces the model to guess. Is this the same as looking up customer info? What does the output include? A detailed description like 'Retrieves order details (order ID, items, total, status, dates, tracking number). Use this to check order status or verify what was ordered. Input: order_id (string). Returns: {id, items: [{sku, qty, price}], total, status, order_date, tracking_number}. Error: 'not_found' if order ID doesn't exist' leaves no ambiguity. The agent knows exactly when to call it and what to expect Domain(s): Tool Design & MCP Integration
