The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.This team's monorepo stores prompt template files with a .prompt.md extension next to each subagent's code, scattered across agents/search/, agents/analysis/, agents/synthesis/, and agents/report/. The team wants Claude Code to follow strict citation-formatting conventions whenever anyone edits these template files, wants the conventions shared with every teammate through the repository, and wants to avoid consuming context in sessions where no template files are touched. What is the most maintainable configuration approach?

choices.text: Place a directory-level CLAUDE.md containing the conventions inside each of the four agent subdirectories.
Add the citation-formatting conventions to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so they are present in every session.
Append the citation-formatting conventions to the root project CLAUDE.md so they are loaded at the start of every session.
Create a rule file in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter setting paths to ["**/*.prompt.md"] and commit it to the repository.

explanation: "The core decision here is choosing the right instruction scope for a convention that applies to files identified by type rather than by location. Claude Code offers several placement options with different loading behaviors: the project root CLAUDE.md loads at the start of every session, directory-level CLAUDE.md files are tied to a single folder and are included when Claude reads files under that folder, user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies only to one developer and never travels with the repository, and rule files in .claude/rules/ can carry YAML frontmatter with a paths glob so they load only when Claude works with matching files.

stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.Your pipeline runs each pull request review as two sequential headless steps on the same runner: the first invocation runs claude -p with –output-format json to analyze the diff and identify risky changes, and a later step in the same job must generate targeted test cases that build directly on the first step's full analysis, including its tool calls and findings. Multiple pull request jobs frequently execute concurrently on this shared runner in the same workspace directory. What is the most reliable way to give the second invocation the first invocation's context?

choices.text: Have the first invocation write its analysis findings into CLAUDE.md so the second invocation loads them as project context at startup.
Run the second invocation with the --continue flag so it automatically picks up the most recent session on the runner.
Issue the second invocation as a fresh command and rely on Claude retaining the first invocation's conversation state server-side.
Capture the session ID from the first invocation's JSON output and pass it to the second invocation using the resume option.

explanation: "In headless and Agent SDK usage, a session is the accumulated conversation history: the prompt, every tool call, every tool result, and every response. The SDK writes this transcript to disk automatically so a later invocation can pick it up, but nothing is retained server-side between runs; each new invocation starts a fresh session unless you explicitly continue or resume one. The mental model is that statefulness is something your pipeline constructs by handing session identity from one step to the next.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.This team wants every engineer to get access to an internal documentation-search MCP server automatically when they clone the repository, so it is defined in a project-level .mcp.json checked into version control. The server's startup command requires an API token for the documentation service, and security policy prohibits committing secrets to the repository. How should the team configure the server?

choices.text: Have each engineer register the server with the token hardcoded in their user-level ~/.claude.json so no configuration file is committed.
Add the token to the project CLAUDE.md so Claude includes it as context and passes it to the server when the connection is established.
Commit the token directly in the .mcp.json entry, since the repository is private and the server only reaches internal documentation.
Reference the token as ${DOCS_API_TOKEN} in the committed .mcp.json entry and have each engineer set that variable in their local environment.

explanation: "Claude Code supports two homes for MCP server configuration with different sharing semantics: a project-level .mcp.json at the repository root, which is committed and distributed to everyone who clones the project, and user-level configuration in ~/.claude.json, which stays private to one machine. The tension in this scenario is that shared configuration files must never carry secrets, yet the server needs a credential to start. The mechanism that resolves this is environment variable expansion: the committed entry references a placeholder such as ${DOCS_API_TOKEN}, and Claude Code substitutes the value from each engineer's local environment at connection time. The configuration travels with the repository; the secret never does.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.One component of your productivity tooling makes a direct Messages API call for each module it analyzes, producing a JSON record with fields like name, purpose, dependencies, and risk_level that a team dashboard ingests. The current prompt simply instructs Claude to "respond with a JSON object containing these fields," but roughly 7% of responses wrap the JSON in explanatory prose or omit required fields, breaking the ingestion pipeline. Which change most reliably ensures the response conforms to the expected schema?

choices.text: Define the module record as a JSON Schema and pass it in the request via output_config.format with type json_schema.
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening curly brace and add a closing-fence stop sequence to force raw JSON.
Embed the full schema as a fenced example in the system prompt and instruct Claude to output only JSON with no surrounding text.
Define an emit_module_record tool whose input_schema matches the record and set tool_choice to "auto" so Claude can call it.

explanation: "Anthropic's structured output support has two distinct mechanisms: JSON outputs, configured through output_config.format with type: "json_schema", which constrain Claude's final response to a supplied JSON Schema, and strict tool use, enabled with strict: true on a tool definition, which validates tool names and tool parameters. For a pipeline that consumes the model's response directly (like this dashboard ingester), output_config.format is the right fit: the structured result comes back as valid JSON inside a text content block, ready to parse.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.Production run logs show that in roughly 9% of runs, the coordinator spawns the report-generation subagent before the synthesis subagent has returned its consolidated findings, producing reports with missing or incomplete citations. Your team decides that synthesis must always complete before report generation begins. Which change most reliably enforces this ordering?

choices.text: Add a PreToolUse hook on the Task tool that denies any spawn of the report-generation subagent until a synthesis findings artifact has been produced.
Revise the coordinator's system prompt to state that the synthesis subagent must always be invoked before the report-generation subagent.
Add few-shot examples to the coordinator's prompt demonstrating the correct sequence of subagent invocations for a typical research run.
Add a PostToolUse hook on the Task tool that detects out-of-order report-generation spawns and returns an error message to the coordinator.

explanation: "This is the classic distinction between probabilistic guidance and deterministic enforcement in agentic workflows. Prompt instructions and few-shot examples shift the odds that Claude follows a required sequence, but they cannot guarantee it; the 9% out-of-order rate is direct evidence that the coordinator's reasoning sometimes deviates. When a workflow constraint is a hard requirement (synthesis output must exist before report generation), the correct architectural move is to encode the prerequisite as code that the model cannot bypass.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your agent spawns subagents to investigate separate areas of an unfamiliar legacy codebase, and each subagent returns a prose summary that a synthesis step combines into an onboarding document. Engineers reviewing the document report two problems: architectural claims have no file references they can verify, and in one case two subagents described the same feature-flag mechanism differently but the final document presented only one version with no mention of the disagreement. What change most effectively addresses both problems?

choices.text: Pass each subagent's full raw exploration transcript into the synthesis agent's context so that no source detail is lost during compression.
Add a post-synthesis verification pass where a second Claude instance re-reads the codebase to attach file references to each claim in the finished document.

Require each subagent to return findings as structured claim-source mappings (claim, file path, code excerpt) that the synthesis step must preserve, annotating any conflicting findings with both sources.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the synthesis agent to include a file citation for every claim in the final document and to select the more plausible finding when subagent reports conflict.

explanation: "In multi-agent synthesis, provenance is lost at the compression step: when a subagent condenses its investigation into a prose summary, the file paths and excerpts that grounded each finding are stripped out, and no downstream instruction or verification pass can reliably reconstruct them. The correct mental model is that attribution is data that must flow through the pipeline, not prose style that can be added at the end. Requiring subagents to emit claim-source mappings (each claim paired with its file path and a supporting excerpt) and requiring the synthesis step to preserve those mappings keeps every statement in the final document independently verifiable.https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/citationshttps://docs.anthropic.com/e n/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinationsThe same structured approach solves the second failure: when two subagents describe the same mechanism differently, the synthesizer should annotate the conflict with both sources rather than arbitrarily choosing one. Silent selection converts a detectable disagreement into an invisible error, whereas an annotated conflict lets an engineer (or a coordinator agent) inspect both cited locations and reconcile them. This mirrors Anthropic's broader guidance on grounding: claims should be tied to direct quotes or exact passages from source material, and unsupported claims should be flagged or retracted rather than presented confidently, because hallucination-mitigation techniques reduce but do not eliminate fabrication.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Your team keeps the agent's MCP tool implementations (including process_refund) in a Git repository, and you want every pull request touching that code to receive an automated Claude Code review during the CI pipeline. A pipeline script must consume the review results programmatically and fail the build when critical issues are detected, with no human involvement in triggering or approving the run. Which approach should you use?

choices.text: Configure the Claude Code GitHub Action without a prompt input so reviewers trigger a review by commenting @claude on each pull request.
Resume a long-lived named review session with claude -r on each pipeline run so the reviewer retains context from all previous reviews.
Start claude in its default interactive mode on the CI runner and pipe the review prompt to it through standard input.
Invoke claude with the -p flag and the review prompt in the pipeline job, using --output-format json so the script can parse the result.

explanation: "Driving Claude Code from a pipeline hinges on one core distinction: interactive sessions assume a human is present to answer questions and grant approvals, while print mode (claude -p or –print) is a one-shot, non-interactive execution model built for automation. The prompt goes in, the result comes out on stdout, and the process exits with a code the pipeline can act on. Adding –output-format json turns the free-form review into structured data, so a downstream script can inspect the findings deterministically and decide whether to fail the build. This is the standard architecture for automated code review, test generation, and other unattended Claude Code tasks in CI/CD.

stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.Your pipeline's code review step depends on a custom MCP server that pulls ticket context from your internal issue tracker so reviews can reference requirements. The engineer who built it registered the server with user scope on their own machine, so reviews work in their sessions, but the server is unavailable to other developers' clones and to the CI runners. Which change most effectively makes the server available consistently across the team and the pipeline?

choices.text: Document the server's startup command in the project's CLAUDE.md so Claude Code launches it automatically whenever a session begins.
Ask each teammate to add the server with local scope in their project directory, keeping the configuration private to each checkout.
Define the server in a project-scoped .mcp.json committed to the repository, using environment variable expansion for the credential.
Add a setup script that runs claude mcp add with user scope on every developer machine and every CI runner during onboarding.

explanation: Claude Code resolves MCP servers from three installation scopes, and choosing the right one is fundamentally a question of who needs the server. Local scope (the default) is private to your copy of one project; user scope lives in ~/.claude.json and follows one person across all their projects; project scope writes to .mcp.json at the repository root, which is meant to be committed so the configuration travels with the code. When a server must be present for every teammate and every CI checkout, project scope is the only option that distributes automatically: cloning or pulling the repo is the installation step.

stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.Your pipeline uses the Claude Agent SDK to review pull requests. The main agent first reads the PR diff and collects the failing CI logs, then delegates deeper analysis to a test-gap-analyzer subagent defined via the agents parameter. In production runs, the subagent's findings describe generic testing best practices and never reference the specific modules that changed in the PR or the failures the main agent already collected. What is the most effective way to fix this?

choices.text: Include the diff summary and the collected failure details directly in the delegation prompt sent to the subagent.
Configure a hook that copies the parent's full message history into the subagent's context window when it is spawned.
Expand the subagent's tools list to match the parent's allowedTools so it inherits the parent session's accumulated state.
Move the diff summary and failure details into the subagent's description field so they load when the subagent is spawned.

explanation: "The core mental model here is context isolation: every non-fork subagent spawned through the SDK begins with a fresh context window. It receives its own system prompt (from its definition), environment details, and the delegation prompt, but it never sees the parent's conversation history, prior tool results, or reasoning. This isolation is the whole point of subagents; it keeps verbose exploration output from flooding the main conversation, but it also means the parent must treat the delegation prompt as the sole data pipe. If the diff summary and CI failure logs are not written into that prompt, they simply do not exist for the subagent, which then falls back on generic patterns rather than the specifics of the PR.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.During an extended session exploring a 300-file legacy billing system, your agent initially reports precise findings (specific module names, dependency chains, and configuration quirks). After roughly two hours of continued exploration, engineers notice it begins describing "typical patterns in billing systems" instead of citing the specific files it examined, and it contradicts findings it reported earlier in the session. You already summarize the conversation history each time it grows large. What change would most effectively preserve the critical findings for the remainder of the session?

choices.text: Add a system prompt instruction directing the agent to answer only from files it has actually examined and never rely on general patterns.
Have the agent write key findings to a scratchpad file as it discovers them and reference that file when answering later questions.
Apply cache_control with type ephemeral to the accumulated exploration history so earlier findings persist across API calls.
Run an additional, more aggressive summarization pass over the conversation history each time the context grows large.

explanation: The failure pattern here is context degradation during extended exploration: as tool results accumulate and history gets summarized, specific discoveries (file names, dependency chains, quirks) get compressed into vaguer and vaguer summaries until the model falls back on generic priors like "typical billing system patterns." Repeated summarization makes this worse, not better, because each pass loses nuance; this is the progressive summarization trap.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Engineers on this team ask the agent to "add comprehensive test coverage to the legacy billing module." Nobody on the team knows which parts of the module are untested, which functions have hidden dependencies, or which behaviors are safe to exercise in tests; that knowledge must come from investigating the code itself. You need to choose a task decomposition strategy for this work. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Skip decomposition and have the main agent load the whole module into context and write all tests in one continuous pass.
Spawn one subagent per source file at the start of the run so each writes tests for its file in parallel, maximizing throughput.
Use dynamic adaptive decomposition, having the agent explore the module first and generate subsequent subtasks based on what each investigation step reveals.
Use a fixed sequential pipeline that applies the same predetermined series of steps to the module, since prompt chaining gives more predictable behavior.

explanation: The core decision here is whether the work can be enumerated upfront. Prompt chaining (a fixed sequential pipeline) predefines the steps and runs them in order; it is the right choice when you can list the work in advance, such as a review that always checks the same aspects. When the shape of the work only emerges as the agent learns, a feedback-driven, agent-style decomposition fits better: the agent investigates, then generates its next subtasks from what it just discovered. Adding comprehensive tests to an unfamiliar legacy module has exactly this character: which functions are untested, which dependencies need stubbing, and which behaviors are exercisable are all facts the agent must uncover before subtasks can even be named.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.To improve quality, the team plans a nightly compliance audit: every resolved conversation from the day (roughly 5,000 transcripts) is re-reviewed by Claude to detect missed escalations and policy violations, with results consumed by the QA team the next morning. Leadership also wants to reduce inference costs wherever possible, including on the live agent's customer-facing calls. Which processing strategy best balances cost and responsiveness?

choices.text: Move both the live agent's customer-facing calls and the nightly transcript audits onto the Message Batches API so the 50% discount applies uniformly to all inference traffic.
Submit the nightly transcript audits through the Message Batches API with a custom_id per transcript, keeping live customer-facing calls on synchronous Messages API requests.
Keep both workloads on synchronous Messages API calls, running the 5,000 audit requests in parallel overnight so all results are ready before the QA team arrives in the morning.
Run the nightly audits inside a single batch as agentic loops, where each batched request calls lookup_order mid-request and receives the tool results before producing its verdict.

explanation: The core design decision for batch processing is classifying each workload as blocking or latency-tolerant. The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at 50% of standard API prices, with most batches finishing in under an hour but no latency guarantee: a batch that does not complete within 24 hours simply expires. That trade (cheap and eventually-done versus immediate) makes it ideal for the nightly transcript audit, where results are only needed the next morning, and disqualifying for live customer turns, where a customer is actively waiting on every response.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your agent uses a custom extraction tool with strict tool use to pull structured metadata (endpoint path, HTTP method, owning team, deprecation date) from legacy service files into a service catalog. The tool's input_schema marks all four fields as required, and a validation-retry loop resends any schema violations to the model with the specific error. During spot checks, engineers discover that for older files that contain no ownership or deprecation information, the extracted JSON passes schema validation but includes plausible-sounding fabricated team names and dates. Which change most effectively addresses this quality problem?

choices.text: Make the owning team and deprecation date fields nullable in the schema so the model can indicate when the source file does not contain that information.
Force the extraction tool with a tool_choice of type tool so every response is guaranteed to invoke the extraction schema.
Add a system prompt instruction stating that the model must never guess and should only report values explicitly present in the source file.
Raise the retry limit and include the full source file alongside the validation error on every retry attempt so the model has more chances to self-correct.

explanation: This scenario illustrates a core distinction in extraction quality work: syntactic validity and semantic accuracy are enforced by different mechanisms. Strict tool use guarantees that the tool input matches the JSON Schema, so the outputs here are structurally perfect. The failure is semantic: the model is fabricating values because the schema demands a value for fields the source files sometimes lack. The mental model to carry is that a schema is not just a format contract; it is also a set of pressures on the model. Marking a field required tells the model it must produce something, and when the source offers nothing, a plausible invention is the path of least resistance.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.An engineer on this team needs Claude Code to diagnose an intermittent data corruption bug in an unfamiliar legacy reconciliation module. Several root causes are plausible, and the team lead requires that the full remediation approach be reviewed before any source files are changed; the engineer still wants Claude to read code and run investigation commands freely. Which workflow best satisfies these requirements?

choices.text: Start the session in plan mode so Claude investigates and proposes a plan, then approve the plan to transition into execution.
Run in acceptEdits mode and instruct Claude in the opening prompt not to modify any files until told, then review changes with git diff afterward.
Run in default (Manual) mode and approve each edit prompt individually as Claude works through the diagnosis and fix.
Run in dontAsk mode with only the read-oriented tools pre-approved so that any edit attempt is automatically denied.

explanation: This situation checks every box for plan mode: the codebase is unfamiliar, multiple valid approaches exist, and a human review gate is required before anything changes on disk. Plan mode is a permission mode, not a prompt convention: while it is active, Claude can read files and explore the repository, but it does not edit source files until the plan is approved. The approval prompt then offers choices for how implementation proceeds (for example, auto-accepting edits or manually reviewing each one), so the workflow naturally moves from investigation to execution in one session.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The document analysis subagent must return each finding as a claim, a supporting evidence excerpt, the source name, and the publication date so the synthesis agent can preserve attribution. Despite a detailed prose description of this format in the subagent's prompt, its outputs still vary: some findings use inline citations, others use footnote-style references, and dates are sometimes omitted, causing the synthesis agent to misattribute claims. What change would most effectively improve output consistency?

choices.text: Add twenty examples that all show the same citation format applied to identical journal-article sources in the prompt.
Enable extended thinking on the subagent so it deliberates about the required citation format before producing each finding.
Rewrite the subagent's prompt with a longer, more detailed prose description of the required citation and date format.
Add three to five diverse examples of correctly formatted findings in example XML tags, one with a missing publication date.

explanation: This situation matches the classic trigger for few-shot prompting: detailed instructions exist, yet the output format remains inconsistent. Prose descriptions of a format are abstract, and the model must translate them into concrete structure on every call, which invites drift (inline citations one time, footnotes the next). A handful of well-crafted examples removes that ambiguity by showing exactly what a correct finding looks like, and Anthropic documents that demonstrating the desired output is more effective than abstract instructions for improving consistency.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your team added three few-shot examples to the agent's boilerplate-generation prompt, all demonstrating REST API controller scaffolding for your primary service framework. Controller output is now highly consistent, but when engineers request other kinds of boilerplate (background workers, database migration scripts), the agent inserts HTTP route handlers and controller-style annotations that do not apply to those artifacts. What change would most effectively resolve this behavior?

choices.text: Expand the example set to 15 or more controller examples to strengthen the pattern signal before addressing other boilerplate types.
Wrap the existing three examples in and XML tags so the agent can better distinguish them from the surrounding instructions.
Remove the few-shot examples and replace them with more detailed prose instructions describing the conventions for each boilerplate type.
Revise the example set to 3-5 diverse examples spanning the boilerplate types engineers request, such as a worker and a migration script.

explanation: Few-shot examples do more than show formatting; the model treats them as evidence of the underlying distribution of tasks it will receive. When every example demonstrates a single artifact type, Claude reasonably infers that controller-style structure is part of the desired output pattern itself, and it carries that pattern into requests where it does not belong. Anthropic's guidance is that examples should be relevant, diverse, and structured, with 3-5 examples that mirror the real use case and cover edge cases; otherwise the model may infer unintended patterns from what the examples have in common.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Human support agents report that escalated tickets from this agent arrive with only a one-line note such as "customer disputes billing charge, please assist," forcing them to re-verify the customer's identity and re-investigate the issue from scratch, which roughly doubles handling time. Your ticketing system creates each ticket directly from the escalate_to_human tool call payload, and human agents have no access to the agent's conversation transcript. Which change most reliably ensures every escalation contains a complete, self-contained handoff?

choices.text: Define the required handoff fields (customer ID, issue, actions taken, recommendation) in the escalate_to_human input schema and validate payloads before ticket creation.
Configure a PostToolUse hook on escalate_to_human that detects sparse payloads and enriches the created ticket with additional case context after the call completes.
Include the raw conversation transcript as a single free-text field in the escalation payload so human agents can review the full interaction history themselves.
Add system prompt instructions directing the agent to always compile a thorough handoff summary covering the case details whenever it decides to escalate to a human.

explanation: Escalation is a handoff, and a handoff is only as good as the artifact it produces. Because the receiving human never sees the agent's conversation transcript, the escalate_to_human payload must be self-contained: who the customer is, what the issue is, what has already been tried, and what the agent recommends. The most reliable way to guarantee that is to encode those requirements in the tool's input schema as required fields (customer ID, issue summary, actions already attempted, recommended next action) and validate the payload before ticket creation. Claude is trained to satisfy tool input schemas, so making the fields required turns "please write a good summary" into a structural precondition of the escalation itself, and validation gives you a deterministic backstop when a payload still comes through thin.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.The team's main agent uses the built-in tools for everyday codebase exploration and boilerplate generation. They recently added a browser-automation MCP server exposing 25 tools to the project's .mcp.json so a specialized ui-testing subagent can verify generated frontend code. Since then, the main agent's context is consumed by the server's tool descriptions on every request, and its selection among the built-in tools has become noticeably less reliable, even though only the ui-testing subagent ever needs the browser tools. Which change most effectively resolves this?

choices.text: Move the browser-automation server out of .mcp.json and define it inline in the ui-testing subagent's definition using its mcpServers configuration.
Keep the server in .mcp.json and rewrite each of the 25 tool descriptions with sharper boundaries stating they apply only to browser testing.
Set tool_choice to "any" for the main agent so it must commit to a single tool call instead of deliberating across the enlarged tool set.
Keep the server in .mcp.json but add its tool patterns to the disallowedTools list so the main agent cannot call them.

explanation: The core principle behind this problem is scoped tool access: every tool definition attached to an agent consumes context on every request and competes for attention during tool selection. When a large MCP server is configured at the project level in .mcp.json, its entire tool catalog is discovered at connection time and injected into the main conversation, even if only one specialized subagent ever uses those tools. As the tool count grows, selection reliability among all tools, including unrelated built-in tools, degrades.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The system's generated reports currently receive full human review before publication, and leadership wants to reduce reviewer workload. A quarterly evaluation shows 96% overall citation accuracy. Reports on niche scientific topics make up only a small fraction of total volume; general news topics account for the rest. Which review workflow design most reliably reduces reviewer effort while maintaining accuracy?

choices.text: Add a second pass where the synthesis agent re-reads its own report and escalates to a reviewer only when it detects problems in its own citations.
Calibrate per-claim confidence scores on a labeled validation set, route low-confidence claims to reviewers, and stratified-sample high-confidence output.
Have the report agent output a single self-assessed confidence score per report and send only reports scoring below a fixed threshold to human reviewers.
Replace full review with a uniform random sample of 10% of reports, treating the 96% aggregate accuracy as sufficient evidence for the remainder.

explanation: Reducing human review safely is fundamentally a confidence calibration problem: the system must know not just what it produced, but how likely each piece of output is to be wrong, and that estimate must be validated against ground truth. The workable pattern is to have agents emit per-claim (or per-field) confidence scores, then use a labeled validation set to discover what those scores actually mean, for example that claims scored below a certain level carry a 20% error rate while those above it carry 1%. Only then can review thresholds be set deliberately rather than by guesswork.

stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.This team's automated review job runs Claude Code against large pull requests, some touching 100+ files across the monorepo. On these large PRs, the review produces specific, well-grounded findings for the first files it analyzes, but comments on later files become vague, reference "typical patterns" rather than the actual code, and occasionally contradict findings made earlier in the same run. What change to the review job most effectively addresses this behavior?

choices.text: Restructure the job into per-file analysis passes that each produce structured findings, followed by a separate pass that loads only those findings to check cross-file consistency.
Add a system prompt instruction directing Claude to give equal attention to every file in the pull request regardless of its position in the review.
Concatenate the full diff and the complete contents of every touched file into a single prompt at the start of the run so all context is available before analysis begins.
Have the job invoke /compact after every ten files so earlier analysis is repeatedly summarized to free space for the remaining files.

explanation: The failure pattern here (specific findings early, generic "typical patterns" commentary later, and self-contradiction within one run) is the signature of context degradation. In Claude Code, the context window is the primary resource to manage: every file read, diff, and prior finding accumulates in it, and performance can degrade as it fills. Reviewing 100+ files in a single continuous session guarantees that later analysis operates against a saturated context where earlier specifics have lost salience.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.In the system described above, the document analysis subagent has two custom MCP tools: search_internal_archive (description: "Searches documents") and search_cached_web_pages (description: "Search function for saved content"). Trace logs show the subagent frequently calls search_cached_web_pages when the requested source material exists only in the internal archive, and vice versa, producing incomplete findings for the synthesis subagent. What is the highest-leverage change to fix this misrouting?

choices.text: Build a routing classifier that analyzes each request and programmatically selects which of the two search tools the subagent may call.
Rename the tools to longer, more descriptive identifiers while keeping the existing descriptions unchanged.
Add a set of few-shot examples to the subagent's system prompt demonstrating correct tool selection for common query types.
Rewrite each tool's description to state exactly what corpus it searches, when to use it, when NOT to use it, and what it returns.

explanation: Claude chooses among available tools by reading their descriptions, which Anthropic documents as the single most important factor in tool performance. A description is not a label; it is the plaintext guidance the model uses to understand what the tool does, when it should and should not be used, what its parameters mean, and what it returns. Anthropic's guidance is to write at least three to four sentences per description, more for complex tools. Descriptions like "Searches documents" and "Search function for saved content" give the model no basis for distinguishing two search tools whose corpora differ, so misrouting is the predictable result.

stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.The pipeline's automated review step asks Claude to return its findings as JSON that your CI code validates against a schema before posting to the pull request. Intermittently, on large pull requests with many findings, the parsing step fails because the JSON output is cut off mid-array. Inspecting the API responses for the failed runs shows stop_reason is "max_tokens". Which change to your validation-retry loop most effectively resolves these failures?

choices.text: Send the truncated JSON and the parser's error message back to Claude in a follow-up request so it can self-correct the malformed output.
Have the loop check stop_reason after each response and, when it is "max_tokens", retry the request with a higher max_tokens value.
Add a system prompt instruction requiring Claude to always emit complete, syntactically valid JSON before ending its response.
Enable strict tool use on the findings tool definition so schema enforcement guarantees well-formed output and removes the need for retry logic.

explanation: The diagnostic clue in this scenario is stop_reason: "max_tokens". Every successful Messages API response includes a stop_reason, and a well-designed pipeline inspects it to decide whether to use the response, retry, or fall back. When the value is max_tokens, the model did not finish; generation was cut off by the output token ceiling, and the documented remedy is to retry with a higher max_tokens. This is a different failure class from a formatting mistake, which is why the fix belongs in your pipeline's control logic rather than in the prompt.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Your team refactors the support agent into a coordinator that delegates to specialized subagents defined programmatically through the Agent SDK's agents parameter, including a billing-dispute subagent with a detailed system prompt covering proration rules, chargeback handling, and refund eligibility. Its AgentDefinition description field reads simply "billing agent." Production traces show that for most billing disputes, the coordinator never invokes this subagent and instead attempts to resolve the dispute itself, often incorrectly. What change would most directly restore correct delegation?

choices.text: Rewrite the subagent's description field to name the billing dispute situations it handles and signal that it should be used proactively.
Move the delegation criteria from the description field into the subagent's system prompt so it explains when the subagent should be invoked.
Convert the programmatic definition to a markdown file in .claude/agents/ so the coordinator can discover the subagent at session start.
Add the Agent tool to the billing-dispute subagent's own tools list so it registers correctly with the coordinator's delegation mechanism.

explanation: In the Agent SDK's coordinator-subagent pattern, the coordinator does not consult a subagent's system prompt when deciding whether to delegate. Delegation is driven by the subagent's description field: Claude compares the task at hand against each registered subagent's description and invokes the one that matches. The system prompt only shapes behavior after invocation, inside the subagent's own fresh context. This split is deliberate: descriptions stay short so the coordinator can evaluate many candidate agents cheaply, while detailed domain instructions live in the subagent where they do not bloat the coordinator's context.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.A developer productivity team uses a Playwright MCP server so their Claude Code agent can run browser-based verification. One engineer registered the server with claude mcp add using the default settings and it works on their machine, but teammates who clone the repository do not get the server at all. The team wants every developer to receive the server configuration automatically when they clone or pull the repo, and they accept that each developer will approve the server once. What should they do?

choices.text: Register the server at project scope so its configuration is written to .mcp.json and committed to version control.
Register the server at user scope in ~/.claude.json so it is available in every session the engineer starts.
Add the claude mcp add command to the project's CLAUDE.md so the server is loaded automatically from the project instructions.
Keep the current local-scope registration and have each teammate run claude mcp reset-project-choices after pulling the repository.

explanation: Claude Code supports three MCP installation scopes, and choosing the right one is what determines who receives a server's configuration. Local scope is the default when running claude mcp add: it is private to the current project for that one user, which is exactly why the engineer's registration never reached teammates. User scope stores private configuration in ~/.claude.json and follows one user across all of their projects. Project scope writes the server entry to .mcp.json at the repository root, a file designed to be committed to version control so the whole team inherits the same tooling automatically on clone or pull.

stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.Your automated PR review workflow invokes Claude Code non-interactively across many services in a single repository. The team has strict security review conventions for database migration SQL files, which live in a migrations folder inside each service (for example, services/billing/migrations/ and services/auth/migrations/). You want these conventions applied whenever a review touches a migration file, but you do not want them consuming context on the many review runs that touch no migrations. What is the most maintainable way to configure this?

choices.text: Create a rule file in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter containing paths: ["**/migrations/*.sql"] and commit it to the repository.
Reference the migration conventions from the root CLAUDE.md using @path/to/file import syntax so they are pulled in only when needed.
Create a rule file in .claude/rules/ without a paths field and state in its content that it applies only to SQL migration files.
Add a CLAUDE.md file inside each service's migrations directory containing the security review conventions.

explanation: Claude Code's path-specific rules exist precisely for this pattern: conventions that matter only for a certain kind of file, where those files are scattered across many directories. A Markdown file in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter such as paths: ["**/migrations/*.sql"] loads its content only when Claude is working with files that match the glob. In a CI review pipeline this has a double benefit: reviews that touch no migrations never pay the token cost of the security conventions, and reviews that do touch migrations get the guidance automatically, without the prompt author remembering to include it.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.An engineer on this team spent yesterday's session having the agent trace the dependency graph of a legacy billing module, and the agent identified 20 files involved in the payment reconciliation flow. Overnight, a teammate merged a refactor that moved and renamed 6 of those files. Today the engineer wants to continue the investigation and produce a final dependency report. What is the most effective way to continue this work?

choices.text: Resume yesterday's named session so the full investigation context is preserved, and let the agent continue building the dependency report from where it left off.
Start a fresh session, injecting a structured summary of yesterday's findings and noting which 6 files were moved so the agent re-verifies those areas.
Start a fresh session with no prior context and have the agent re-trace the entire dependency graph from scratch against the current state of the codebase.
Resume yesterday's session and immediately run /compact so the accumulated exploration output is condensed before continuing the dependency investigation.

explanation: The core decision when continuing multi-day codebase investigations is resume versus start fresh, and it hinges on whether the prior session's tool results are still valid. Claude has no live view of the filesystem between turns; everything it "knows" about the codebase comes from Read, Grep, and Bash outputs frozen into the conversation at the moment they ran. When the underlying code changes, that evidence silently becomes stale, and a resumed agent will keep reasoning from it with full confidence because nothing in the context signals that the repository moved on.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Human agents who receive escalations from this agent report a recurring problem with the case summaries the agent attaches. In one billing dispute, the summary stated that a refund had already been issued, but that claim came only from the customer's message; the lookup_order result actually showed no refund on record. Reviewers say they cannot tell which statements in a summary came from backend tool results and which came from the customer, so they must re-investigate every case from scratch. What change would most effectively fix the escalation summaries?

choices.text: Have the agent append an overall confidence score to each escalation summary so reviewers know how much scrutiny each case requires before acting.
Add a second summarization pass that condenses the full case history into a shorter, cleaner narrative before the summary is sent to the human agent.
Instruct the agent to treat backend tool results as authoritative and omit any customer statements that contradict system records from the escalation summary.
Require each fact in the summary to cite its origin (customer statement or specific tool result) and annotate conflicts between the two with attribution.

explanation: Core Failure: Loss of Information ProvenanceThe agent draws on two distinct source types: verified backend records (e.g., lookup_order) and unverified customer assertions. Summaries flatten both into undifferentiated prose, preventing downstream human reviewers from distinguishing system facts from customer statements and forcing them to re-investigate every case.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The web search and document analysis subagents in this system call three different MCP tools that return timestamps in inconsistent formats: one returns Unix epoch integers, one returns strings like "March 31, 2026", and one returns ISO 8601 strings. As a result, the synthesis subagent sometimes mis-orders findings chronologically. Which approach most reliably ensures the agents always reason over consistent timestamp formats?

choices.text: Register a PreToolUse hook that uses updatedInput to rewrite each outgoing tool call so the MCP servers return timestamps in ISO 8601 format.
Register a PostToolUse hook matched to those MCP tools that converts all timestamps in the tool response to ISO 8601 before the result enters the agent's context.
Add explicit instructions to each subagent's system prompt directing it to convert every timestamp it encounters to ISO 8601 before comparing dates.
Register a SubagentStop hook that scans each subagent's final summary and rewrites any inconsistently formatted dates before it returns to the coordinator.

explanation: Core Issue: Reasoning Corruption via Inconsistent Tool DataHeterogeneous tool results entering the model's context can corrupt downstream reasoning if inconsistencies exist.

stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.Your pipeline includes a job that generates unit tests for each pull request using claude -p. The CI runner has the project's full build and test dependencies installed, and the job's permission configuration allows Claude Code to execute the test command and read its output. Engineers report that a meaningful share of the generated tests either fail to compile or fail immediately when run against the current code, forcing them to fix the tests manually before merging. Which refinement to the test-generation job would most effectively improve the reliability of the generated tests?

choices.text: Include two or three few-shot examples of well-structured test cases in the prompt so Claude follows a proven pattern.
Ask Claude to review its generated tests at the end of the run and confirm they appear correct before finishing.
Add an instruction to the project CLAUDE.md stating that all generated tests must compile and pass before being committed.
Update the job's prompt to have Claude run the generated tests, read the failures, and iterate until the suite passes.

explanation: Core Principle: Grounding Progress in Verifiable ChecksIterative refinement with Claude Code requires measuring progress against verifiable checks (tests, build exit codes, linters, fixture diffs) rather than plausible-sounding output. Instructing Claude to run generated tests and iterate on failures grounds each loop in objective compiler/runtime feedback, terminating on a concrete passing condition. In a CI context where human oversight is absent, this self-correction loop must be embedded directly into the prompt and job execution.

You want the agent to reliably distinguish between findings it should post automatically and findings that should be routed to a human reviewer for a judgment call. Have the agent attach a self-reported confidence score to each finding and automatically route any finding below a fixed threshold to a human reviewer.
Add explicit escalation criteria to the review prompt, with few-shot examples demonstrating which findings to route to a human versus post automatically.

The most reliable implementation uses explicit escalation criteria backed by few-shot examples showing concrete cases on both sides of the boundary:

A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.Your team develops this system in a monorepo where each subagent lives in its own package (agents/search, agents/analysis, agents/synthesis, agents/report), and TypeScript test files (*.test.ts) sit next to the code they verify in every package. You want Claude Code to apply the team's testing conventions whenever it works with test files, while keeping always-loaded context to a minimum. Which approach best meets both goals?

choices.text: Create a rule file in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter listing paths: ["**/*.test.ts"] so it loads only for matching files.
Create a testing rule file in .claude/rules/ without any frontmatter, relying on the rules directory to scope it automatically.
Add the testing conventions to a standards file and reference it from the root CLAUDE.md with an @import so all packages receive it.
Place a directory-level CLAUDE.md file containing the testing conventions inside each of the four agent package directories.

explanation: Core Architecture: Path-Specific RulesClaude Code's .claude/rules/ directory uses Markdown files with a paths YAML frontmatter field (e.g., paths: ["**/*.test.ts"]) to enable conditional context loading. Instructions load into memory only when working on files matching those glob patterns, saving tokens during unrelated tasks.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Your agent handles a complex billing dispute spanning 45 turns, during which the customer references two orders, states a preferred resolution (partial refund to the original card), and negotiates an adjusted amount of $83.50. Your application summarizes older conversation history each time it approaches a size threshold. Logs show that after the third summarization pass, the agent quotes an incorrect refund amount and asks the customer to restate the resolution they already chose, damaging the interaction. What change would most effectively prevent this loss of critical information?

choices.text: Instruct the agent to call get_customer and lookup_order at the start of every turn to refresh the relevant order and account details from backend systems.
Extract transactional facts (amounts, order numbers, customer-stated preferences) into a case facts block included in every prompt and excluded from summarization.
Apply cache_control markers to the older conversation history so prompt caching preserves those earlier turns and their details across subsequent API calls.
Raise the size threshold that triggers summarization so that fewer compression passes occur before a typical billing dispute conversation concludes.

explanation: This failure is the progressive summarization trap: each summarization pass loses nuance, and after several rounds, critical details like a negotiated dollar amount or a customer's stated preference are diluted beyond usefulness. Because Claude is stateless, the model only knows what your application includes in the current request; if a fact was compressed out of the summary, it is simply gone from the model's perspective.

A Markdown file in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter such as paths: ["**/migrations/*.sql"] loads its content only when Claude is working with files that match the glob. stem: SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.Your pipeline runs automated PR reviews with claude -p using the –bare flag so every run starts identically regardless of the runner's local configuration. The repository contains a pr-security-reviewer subagent defined as a Markdown file in .claude/agents/, and developers confirm the subagent is delegated to correctly in their local interactive sessions. In CI logs, however, the subagent is never spawned and the main agent performs all analysis itself, consuming most of the context window. What change restores subagent delegation in CI while preserving the pipeline's requirement for consistent, configuration-independent startup?

choices.text: Add an @-mention of pr-security-reviewer to the -p prompt to guarantee the subagent is invoked.
Pass the subagent definition explicitly to the headless invocation using the --agents flag.
Remove the --bare flag from the invocation so the run auto-discovers the repository's .claude/agents/ directory.
Copy the subagent definition to ~/.claude/agents/ on the CI runner so it loads at user scope.

explanation: The key to this failure is understanding what –bare actually does. Bare mode exists to make headless runs deterministic: it skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so nothing configured on a particular machine or in a teammate's home directory can silently change a CI run's behavior. The tradeoff is that everything the run needs must be supplied explicitly through flags: –agents for custom subagent definitions, –mcp-config for MCP servers, –settings for settings, and so on. The subagent works locally because interactive sessions auto-discover .claude/agents/; it fails in CI because bare mode never reads that directory.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Your team adds a PreToolUse hook to this agent that intercepts process_refund calls and normalizes the amount field, since the agent sometimes passes amounts as strings like "$45.00" instead of numeric values. The hook matches on process_refund and returns updatedInput containing just the corrected amount field. After deployment, every intercepted process_refund call fails schema validation because order_id and customer_id are missing from the tool input. What change fixes this behavior?

choices.text: Return the corrected amount in the hook's additionalContext field so Claude reissues the tool call with the normalized value.
Have the hook return an updatedInput object that includes the original order_id and customer_id fields alongside the normalized amount.
Move the normalization logic to a PostToolUse hook so the corrected amount is applied after the tool input has been fully assembled.
Set the hook's permissionDecision to allow so the runtime merges updatedInput with the original tool input before execution.

explanation: PreToolUse hooks in the Claude Agent SDK are the right place for input normalization: they run after Claude has constructed the tool parameters but before the tool executes, and can return updatedInput to rewrite the call deterministically. The critical detail this scenario tests is that updatedInput is a full replacement of the tool input object, not a patch. If the hook returns only the field it changed, every other field (here, order_id and customer_id) is silently dropped, which is exactly why the downstream schema validation started failing the moment the hook shipped. The correct pattern is to copy the incoming tool_input, overwrite the fields you are normalizing, and return the complete new object.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The report generation stage in this system produces reports that often exceed 30 pages with dozens of citations. Currently, a single reviewer agent receives the entire completed report in one pass and is asked to verify that every citation supports its claim and that statistics are consistent throughout. Quality audits show the reviewer reliably catches problems in the report's opening sections, frequently misses citation errors in the middle and later sections, and occasionally issues contradictory findings about the same statistic. Which architectural change would most effectively improve review reliability?

choices.text: Have the report generator agent review its own report within its generation conversation before handoff, since it retains full context on every citation.
Enable extended thinking for the reviewer agent so it reasons more deliberately over the entire completed report within a single review pass.
Run the same full-report review three times in parallel with separate reviewer instances and merge the union of all findings from the three runs.
Split the review into independent per-section passes that verify citations locally, plus a separate pass that checks statistics for cross-section consistency.

explanation: The failure pattern in this system, reliable findings early in the document, missed errors in the middle and end, and contradictory conclusions about the same statistic, is characteristic of attention dilution when a single reviewer must process a very long artifact in one pass. Long inputs suffer from positional effects: content buried deep in a large context receives less effective attention, so citation errors on page 22 are systematically less likely to be caught than errors on page 2.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.During development, the team prototyped the coordinator's control loop directly against the Claude API. The loop terminates when the assistant's text response contains the phrase "RESEARCH COMPLETE". In testing, some runs end prematurely when a synthesized finding happens to include that phrase, while other runs never terminate because the model phrases its conclusion differently. Which change most reliably fixes the loop termination logic?

choices.text: Inspect stop_reason on each response, continuing the loop on tool_use and terminating on end_turn, keeping an iteration cap only as a safety net.
Terminate the loop when the assistant's latest response contains structured report elements such as section headers, citation markers, and a conclusion.
Strengthen the system prompt so the model outputs the exact phrase "RESEARCH COMPLETE" only once, on its own line, when the report is fully finished.
Replace the phrase check with a fixed cap of 25 iterations so every research run terminates deterministically after a bounded number of turns.

explanation: Every response from the Claude API carries a stop_reason field that states why generation halted, and this field is the canonical driver of an agentic loop. When stop_reason is tool_use, Claude is requesting a tool execution: the application runs the tool, appends the result to the messages array, and calls the API again. When it is end_turn, Claude has decided the task is done and the loop should exit. Because this is structured metadata emitted by the API rather than prose emitted by the model, it cannot collide with content that happens to appear in research findings, which is exactly the failure the team observed.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The document analysis subagent in this system emits findings by calling an extract_findings tool whose input_schema marks claim, evidence_excerpt, source_name, and publication_date as required for every finding. An audit reveals that when a source document contains no publication date, the subagent fills publication_date with a plausible-looking but fabricated date, which corrupts the temporal reconciliation logic in the final reports. What change most effectively addresses this behavior?

choices.text: Set tool_choice to force the extract_findings tool on every request so schema compliance is guaranteed for each finding.
Make publication_date nullable in the tool's input_schema and instruct the model to return null when the source contains no date.
Add a validation-retry loop that detects suspicious dates and returns the validation error to the subagent for self-correction.
Strengthen the subagent's system prompt with an explicit rule that publication dates must never be invented and must appear verbatim in the source.

explanation: Enforcing structured output through a tool's input_schema guarantees syntactic compliance: the JSON will parse and match the declared shape. It does not guarantee semantic correctness. In fact, an overly strict schema can actively cause semantic errors: when a field is marked required but the source document has no corresponding information, the model's only way to satisfy the schema is to fabricate a value. This is exactly the failure pattern in the audit, and it is why schema design guidance recommends making fields optional or nullable whenever source documents may legitimately lack that information.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Your support agent runs as a Python Agent SDK service on an autoscaled container fleet, and each customer contact may be routed to a different container instance. When a customer follows up on an open billing dispute two days later, the agent must resume the original conversation, including all prior tool calls and reasoning, even though the follow-up request lands on a container that never handled the customer before. Session IDs are stored in your case management database. What should you implement so the agent can reliably resume the prior session on any container?

choices.text: Pass continue_conversation=True on the follow-up query so the SDK automatically locates and resumes the customer's previous session.
Keep each customer's session open with a ClaudeSDKClient instance so context carries over automatically to their next contact.
Mirror session transcripts to shared storage with a SessionStore adapter and resume the stored session ID on the handling container.
Fork the original session on the new container so the follow-up begins with a copy of the prior conversation history.

explanation: In the Claude Agent SDK, a session is the accumulated conversation history: the prompt, every tool call, every tool result, and every response. The SDK writes this transcript to local disk automatically (under ~/.claude/projects//*.jsonl by default), which works well on a single developer machine but breaks down in fleet deployments: a session file written on one container simply does not exist on another, so resume with a valid session ID fails anywhere except the original host.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. The report generation subagent's output must satisfy a documented quality rubric: every claim must cite a source, statistics must include publication dates, and no section may contain unsupported conclusions. Currently, a reviewer agent performs a single pass over each draft report, flags rubric violations, and hands the list to the report generator, which applies fixes and immediately delivers the revised report. Audits show that roughly 20% of delivered reports still violate the rubric because the revisions themselves introduce new unsupported claims that are never re-checked. Which architectural change would most effectively ensure reports meet the rubric before delivery?

choices.text: Route each revised report back through a separate evaluator instance that re-checks it against the rubric, repeating the generate-evaluate cycle until it passes or an iteration cap is reached.
Have the report generator perform a self-review against the rubric within the same response after applying fixes, before delivering the revised report.
Run three parallel reviewer instances with different prompts on the initial draft and aggregate their findings before the generator applies its fixes.
Add the full rubric along with few-shot examples of compliant and non-compliant claims to the report generator's system prompt so revisions are less likely to introduce violations.

explanation: The core insight in this scenario is identifying where in the pipeline quality is being lost. The reviewer catches violations in the draft, but the revised report exits the system unverified, so the architecture has an open loop: feedback flows in one direction and no component confirms that fixes actually resolved the violations without creating new ones.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.A developer on this team creates a shared project skill at .claude/skills/generate-api-docs/SKILL.md containing the team's documentation-generation procedure. In the YAML frontmatter they set name: docgen, expecting teammates to invoke it as /docgen. After committing and pulling, everyone sees only /generate-api-docs in the slash menu, and /docgen is not recognized. What should the developer do so the skill is invoked as /docgen?

choices.text: Add user-invocable: true to the frontmatter so the name field is registered in the slash menu.
Rename the skill directory to .claude/skills/docgen/ so the directory name defines the slash command.
Have each teammate restart Claude Code so the updated frontmatter name is picked up and registered as the command.
Move the file to .claude/commands/generate-api-docs.md so the frontmatter name field determines the command name.
