The reliable fix is to make the escalation decision explicit rather than implicit. By writing concrete criteria for ambiguity into the coordinator's instructions (multiple named entities could match, the analysis dimension is unstated, the time window is unclear) and pairing them with few-shot examples that contrast requests warranting clarification with requests that should proceed, you give the model an observable decision boundary it can pattern-match against. Contrasting examples are consistently more effective than prose rules alone at communicating this kind of judgment, as described in Use examples (multishot prompting).

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The document analysis subagent processes batches of 40 or more lengthy source documents within a single extended session. Logs show that for the first dozen documents, its extracted claims quote specific passages and cite the correct source names, but later in the session it begins attributing claims to the wrong documents and describing findings in generic terms rather than quoting actual content. Which change most effectively addresses this degradation?

choices.text: Have the subagent append each document's key claims, excerpts, and source names to a scratchpad file, then reference it when processing later documents.
Concatenate all source documents into a single initial request so the subagent sees the complete corpus at once instead of processing sequentially.
After each document, summarize the entire conversation so far and replace the accumulated history with that summary before processing the next document.
Enable extended thinking for the subagent so it reasons more deliberately about which source each extracted claim came from before recording it.

explanation: "The symptoms here (accurate, specific extraction early in a session that decays into misattribution and generic statements later) are the classic signature of context degradation in extended sessions. The context window is the primary resource an agent has to work with: every document read, every tool result, and every response accumulates there, and as it fills, the model attends less reliably to earlier material. Details in the middle of a long context are especially vulnerable, which is why claim-source associations, which depend on precise pairings of text and provenance, are among the first things to break down.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.To reduce reviewer workload before reports are published, the team plans to have the synthesis subagent attach a confidence score to each cited claim, auto-publish claims above a threshold, and route only low-confidence claims to human reviewers. Reviewers worry that the model may be confidently wrong on obscure research topics where it hallucinates plausible-sounding claims. Which design change most reliably addresses this concern?

choices.text: Raise the auto-publication threshold so that only claims the model rates near maximum confidence bypass human review.
Have the synthesis subagent re-evaluate its own high-confidence claims with extended thinking enabled before they are auto-published.
Scan each claim's text for hedging phrases such as likely or possibly, and route claims containing that language to human reviewers.
Calibrate the confidence scores against a labeled validation set, then apply stratified random sampling to the auto-published claims.

explanation: The core issue in this design is that a model's self-reported confidence is not the same thing as measured accuracy. Language models tend to be poorly calibrated on exactly the cases that matter most: obscure or hard topics where they produce fluent, confident, but wrong claims. Any workflow that routes items to humans based solely on raw confidence scores inherits this miscalibration, no matter where the threshold is set.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your team defines a legacy-explainer subagent programmatically through the SDK's agents parameter. Its job is to explore unfamiliar legacy modules and return architecture summaries to the main agent. During a pilot run, logs show the subagent used Edit to modify a configuration file while investigating a build issue. The team requires a guarantee that this subagent can analyze code but can never modify files or execute commands. Which configuration change satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Set the subagent's disallowedTools field to Edit, since that is the tool the pilot logs show being misused.
Add explicit instructions to the subagent's system prompt stating that it must never edit files or run shell commands.
Set the subagent's tools field to only Read, Grep, and Glob so modification and execution tools are absent from its session.
Tighten the main agent's allowedTools list, since subagents are constrained to whichever tools the coordinator has pre-approved.

explanation: "The core architectural principle here is the difference between capability removal and behavioral guidance. When a subagent is defined with an explicit tools list, any tool omitted from that list is simply not present in the subagent's session: Claude never sees its definition, so there is no call to intercept, block, or approve. A read-only analysis role gets Read, Grep, and Glob, and the question of whether it might edit a file becomes structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. This is the standard pattern for role-scoped tool distribution: each subagent receives only the tools its role needs, which both hardens safety and improves selection reliability by shrinking the decision space.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.The refund-handling code in this system is spread across several directories: the process_refund MCP tool wrapper lives in src/tools/, refund policy checks live in src/policies/, and their test files sit alongside them, with every filename containing "refund". A teammate documented the team's strict audit-logging and idempotency conventions for this code in .claude/rules/refund-conventions.md, but developers notice the full conventions load into every Claude Code session, even when they are working only on unrelated escalation logic. What change makes these conventions load only when they are relevant?

choices.text: Move refund-conventions.md into a .claude/rules/refunds/ subdirectory so its location restricts it to refund-related work.
Reference the file from the project CLAUDE.md as an @.claude/rules/refund-conventions.md import so it is pulled in only when needed.
Add YAML frontmatter to refund-conventions.md with a paths field containing glob patterns such as **/*refund* that match the refund-related files.
Create a directory-level CLAUDE.md containing the conventions in each directory that holds refund-related files.

explanation: "Files in .claude/rules/ support an optional YAML frontmatter block with a paths field containing glob patterns. When present, the rule's content applies only when Claude is working with files that match; when absent, the rule loads unconditionally at launch and carries the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md. That distinction is exactly what this team is missing: the file exists in the right directory, but without a paths field it behaves like always-on project memory rather than a conditional rule.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Engineers ask the agent to produce an architecture overview of a 500,000-line legacy monorepo, covering the service layer, the data access layer, the public API surface, and the build tooling. In a single session, the agent runs dozens of Grep, Glob, and Read calls, but by the time it writes the overview, the output describes "typical patterns" instead of the specific findings from earlier exploration and misattributes several modules. How should you redesign the task decomposition to fix this?

choices.text: Delegate the entire exploration and synthesis to one general-purpose subagent so the main conversation stays clean, and have it return the finished overview.
Decompose the overview into independent investigation areas and spawn a parallel subagent per area, each returning a concise summary the main agent synthesizes.
Break the exploration into sequential batches of directories processed alphabetically within the same session, completing each batch before starting the next.
Keep all exploration in the main agent's session and run /compact whenever the context window fills, then have the agent synthesize the overview from the compacted history.

explanation: "The failure described here is context degradation: in a long single-session exploration, dozens of raw Grep, Glob, and Read results pile up in the context window, and the model's synthesis drifts from specific observations toward generic priors ('typical patterns'). The architectural fix is to decompose the task along its natural seams (service layer, data layer, API surface, build tooling) and delegate each area to a subagent with its own fresh context window.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Your team is using Claude Code to implement the escalation decision logic that determines when this agent should call escalate_to_human instead of process_refund. Over three iterations, you described the escalation policy in prose, Claude implemented it faithfully, and only while reviewing the resulting behavior did you discover scenarios you had never considered (chargebacks already in dispute, refund requests exceeding a customer's lifetime spend, repeat contacts within 24 hours). You conclude the gaps are in your own understanding of the escalation domain, not in Claude's compliance with your instructions. Which refinement approach would most effectively break this cycle?

choices.text: Provide two or three concrete input and output examples of escalation decisions in the prompt so the expected behavior is communicated unambiguously.
Write a test suite covering the escalation policy first, then share failing test output so Claude iterates until every test passes.
Switch to plan mode so Claude presents its full implementation approach for your review and approval before making any file edits.
Have Claude interview you with questions about escalation edge cases and policy boundaries, then implement based on your answers.

explanation: "Iterative refinement techniques are not interchangeable; each one targets a different source of error, and choosing well starts with diagnosing where the gap actually lives. When Claude misinterprets a rule you understand perfectly, concrete input/output examples communicate the transformation unambiguously. When outputs fail against known criteria, verifiable checks such as tests let Claude iterate until they pass. But when the failure pattern is that you only recognize requirements after seeing the output, the missing knowledge is on your side of the collaboration, and no amount of clearer instruction or tighter verification can encode requirements you have not yet discovered.https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practiceshttps://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflowsThe interview pattern inverts the usual flow: instead of you specifying and Claude implementing, Claude asks questions first. A model that has seen many escalation and refund systems will probe for boundary conditions (disputed charges, spend thresholds, repeat-contact windows) that a developer new to the domain would not think to specify. This moves discovery from post-implementation review, where each missed case costs a full iteration, to a cheap up-front conversation. It pairs naturally with plan mode afterward: interview to establish requirements, plan to structure the implementation, then execute.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.In production, this agent resolves near-identical billing dispute edge cases inconsistently: for the same pattern (a duplicate charge on a partially used subscription), it sometimes issues a full refund via process_refund and other times applies an account credit. The system prompt already contains a detailed decision matrix for billing disputes, and the agent follows it correctly on routine cases. Which change would most effectively improve decision consistency on these ambiguous cases?

choices.text: Define a decide_resolution tool with an enum of allowed resolution actions and use tool_choice to force the agent to call it for every billing dispute.
Add 3-5 examples of the ambiguous dispute types, each showing the case facts, the chosen resolution, and reasoning for rejecting the plausible alternative.
Extend the decision matrix in the system prompt with additional conditional rules that explicitly enumerate every edge-case combination observed in production so far.
Add a dozen examples of clear-cut refund approvals and denials drawn from routine disputes to reinforce the standard policy decision patterns.

explanation: The failure pattern here is a classic signal for few-shot prompting: detailed instructions produce correct behavior on routine cases but inconsistent judgment on ambiguous edge cases. Rules describe policy in the abstract, but they cannot fully specify how to weigh competing considerations when two resolutions (full refund versus account credit) both look defensible. Examples work differently: by showing the case facts, the decision, and the reasoning for rejecting the plausible alternative, they demonstrate the decision boundary itself, which the model can then generalize to novel but similar disputes. Anthropic's guidance is to provide roughly 3-5 relevant, diverse, structured examples that closely mirror the real use case and cover edge cases, ideally wrapped in and tags so Claude can distinguish them from instructions, and it explicitly documents that showing examples of desired output is more effective than abstract instructions for improving consistency.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.An engineer on this team just finished a two-hour Claude Code session refactoring the authentication module. The session's context window is nearly full of file reads, test output, and refactoring discussion. The engineer now needs to start a completely unrelated task in the same repository: generating API documentation for the reporting module. What is the most effective way to manage context before beginning the new task?

choices.text: Append the documentation task's instructions to the project CLAUDE.md so they take precedence over the existing conversation.
Run /clear to reset the conversation context, then start the documentation task with a fresh prompt.
Continue in the same session and rely on automatic compaction to summarize the context as it approaches the limit.
Run /compact so a summary of the refactoring session carries forward into the documentation task.

explanation: "In Claude Code, the context window is the primary resource to manage: it accumulates the conversation, file reads, command output, and instructions, and performance can degrade as it fills. The right context command depends on whether the next task is related to what came before. /compact summarizes the session so relevant history carries forward, which is valuable when continuing the same investigation. /clear resets the conversation entirely, which is the documented choice when switching to an unrelated task, exactly the situation here: nothing from an authentication refactor helps document a reporting module, so a summary of it is pure overhead.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your team adds a PreToolUse hook to this agent to protect auto-generated code from manual modification. The hook uses the matcher "Write|Edit" and its callback returns a deny decision through hookSpecificOutput whenever tool_input.file_path starts with "generated/". In testing, logging confirms the callback fires for every Write and Edit call, but the prefix check always evaluates false, and the agent continues editing files inside the generated/ directory. What change fixes this hook?

choices.text: Change the matcher to "Write(generated/)|Edit(generated/)" so the hook fires only for Write and Edit calls that target the protected directory.
Join the cwd from the hook input with the generated/ directory and compare that absolute path, since file_path is resolved before PreToolUse hooks run.
Move the callback to a PermissionRequest hook, since deny decisions through hookSpecificOutput are only enforced at the permission-decision point.
Register the callback under PostToolUse with the same matcher, since that event receives the finalized tool_input after all path resolution completes.

explanation: "This scenario tests a documented gotcha in Agent SDK hook design: path normalization happens before your hook runs. For the Write, Edit, and Read tools, tool_input.file_path arrives at a PreToolUse callback already expanded to an absolute path; tildes and relative paths are resolved first. A callback that checks file_path.startswith("generated/") therefore never matches, because the actual value looks like /home/dev/project/generated/client.ts. The reliable pattern is to construct the protected directory's absolute path from the cwd field included in the hook input and compare resolved paths (on Windows, also normalizing separators, since paths arrive with backslashes).

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team wrote a helper script, invoked from a custom slash command, that sends each merged change to the Messages API for triage. The request defines three tools (classify_refactor, classify_bugfix, classify_feature), each with an input_schema describing structured metadata for that change type, and the change type is not known in advance. In production, the model occasionally responds with plain-text analysis instead of calling any tool, which breaks the downstream parser. Which change guarantees a structured tool call while still letting the model pick the appropriate schema?

choices.text: Keep tool_choice at its default {"type": "auto"} and add a system prompt instruction stating that every response must be a tool call, never plain text.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so the model is required to call a tool but can select whichever of the three classification tools fits the change.
Add strict: true to each of the three tool definitions so responses are constrained to valid tool calls.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_refactor"} so every request is guaranteed to produce a structured tool call.

explanation: "The failure here is not malformed tool inputs; it is that the model sometimes chooses to answer in prose at all. That choice is governed by tool_choice, which has distinct modes with different guarantees: {"type": "auto"} lets Claude decide whether to use a tool, {"type": "any"} requires Claude to call some tool while leaving the selection to the model, and a forced selection ({"type": "tool", "name": "…"}) pins the response to one specific tool. When multiple extraction schemas exist and the input type varies, {"type": "any"} is the setting that combines a hard guarantee of structured output with flexible routing.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The document analysis subagent in this system is prompted with: "Only report findings that are well-supported by the sources you analyze." An audit of recent reports shows that roughly 20% of findings passed to the synthesis agent attribute claims to documents that never actually state them, and these fabricated attributions flow through into the final cited reports. Which prompt change to the document analysis subagent would most effectively reduce these unsupported findings?

choices.text: Strengthen the instruction to "be extremely conservative and report only findings you are highly certain are completely accurate," emphasizing that accuracy matters more than coverage.
Have the subagent attach a self-reported confidence score from 1 to 10 to each finding, and configure the synthesis agent to discard any finding scored below 7.
Require every finding to include a verbatim supporting quote and source identifier, and instruct the subagent to omit or mark as unverifiable any claim it cannot pair with a direct quote.
Define an extraction tool with a JSON schema containing claim and source fields, and force the subagent to emit all findings through that tool for schema conformance.

explanation: "The failure here is semantic, not structural: the subagent is producing findings in the right shape but attributing claims that the source documents never made. The prompt's criterion, 'well-supported,' is a subjective standard the model interprets differently on every document, so there is nothing forcing each finding to be anchored to actual source text.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.To improve reliability, this team added an independent reviewer: a second Claude instance with no access to the support agent's conversation or reasoning context that must approve every agent response before it is delivered. Audits confirm the reviewer catches flawed decisions effectively, but median response time has roughly doubled, and customers asking simple order-status questions now complain about slow replies. Which change best preserves the review architecture's error-catching value while addressing the latency problem?

choices.text: Gate only high-impact irreversible actions such as process_refund calls behind the independent reviewer, and let low-impact read-only responses like order-status answers proceed without a review pass.
Submit the review passes through the Message Batches API so reviews complete asynchronously without blocking customer responses.
Have the support agent self-report a confidence score with each response and route only low-confidence responses through the independent reviewer.
Replace the independent reviewer with a self-review step inside the support agent's own conversation so the second API call is eliminated.

explanation: Review architectures involve a fundamental tradeoff: every additional pass improves reliability but adds latency and cost. The right design applies review proportionally to risk rather than uniformly. A useful mental model classifies agent actions along two axes, reversibility and impact: a read-only order-status lookup is low impact and trivially correctable, so a review gate adds latency without meaningful protection, while process_refund is irreversible and financially consequential, so a pre-execution review pass is exactly where an independent instance earns its cost. Gating only high-stakes tool calls keeps the reviewer where audits show it works and restores fast responses for the bulk of traffic.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.You are using Claude Code interactively to refine the report-generation subagent's prompt and formatting logic. Three separate times in the same session you have corrected Claude on the same issue: it keeps reintroducing numbered inline citations even though the reports require author-date citations. After each correction the next output looks right, but the problem resurfaces a few turns later, and the conversation now contains a long history of failed attempts and contradictory revisions. What is the most effective next step?

choices.text: Restate the citation correction in the same session with progressively stronger and more emphatic wording each time the issue recurs.
Add the author-date citation rule to the project CLAUDE.md and continue in the current session, expecting the rule to take effect immediately.
Run /clear and start a fresh session with an initial prompt that explicitly states the author-date citation requirement up front.
Run /compact to condense the conversation history into a summary, then continue issuing the same correction in the compacted session.

explanation: "Iterative refinement with Claude Code works best when you recognize that the conversation itself is part of the system's state. Every failed attempt, contradictory revision, and correction stays in the context window and continues to influence subsequent outputs. When Claude fixes an issue and then regresses a few turns later, the usual culprit is not that Claude ignored you; it is that the context now contains competing signals, including the very examples of the wrong citation style you are trying to eliminate.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Production transcripts show that when customers raise several unrelated issues in a single message (for example, disputing a charge, asking about a pending return, and requesting an account email change), the agent thoroughly resolves the first issue but gives vague or incomplete answers on the others, and occasionally mixes order details between issues. You want to redesign how the agent decomposes these requests. Which approach best addresses this failure pattern?

choices.text: Add an upstream classifier that detects messages containing more than one distinct issue and routes those conversations directly to the escalate_to_human tool.
Have the agent first enumerate the customer's distinct issues into a structured list, then resolve each issue one at a time with a tracked status before composing the final response.
Spawn a parallel subagent for each detected issue and rely on each subagent's access to the shared conversation history to resolve its issue with full customer context.
Strengthen the system prompt with an explicit instruction to answer every part of the customer's message completely, and raise the maximum output token limit for longer replies.

explanation: "Multi-issue customer messages are a decomposition problem, not a prompting or capacity problem. When an agent processes a blended request in a single pass, attention concentrates on the most salient issue, later issues get shallow treatment, and facts retrieved for one issue (order numbers, amounts) can leak into another. The fix is to make the decomposition explicit: enumerate the distinct issues first, then resolve each one sequentially with its own investigation and a tracked status, and only synthesize the combined reply after every issue is addressed. This is the same 'decompose, work each subtask in focus, then integrate' pattern that applies across agentic workflows, and it fits naturally inside the SDK's execution loop, where Claude alternates tool calls and reasoning until the task is complete (see the agent loop): https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.Beyond its MCP tools, the agent has Bash access so it can run a case-archival shell script after a resolution completes. Production logs show the agent first issues a Bash call running export CASE_ID=CS-88213, then in a later Bash call runs ./scripts/archive_case.sh, which fails with the error "CASE_ID not set". What change most reliably fixes the archival step?

choices.text: Run the export from within the project directory, since shell state set inside the project scope carries over to later Bash commands the way a directory change does.
Have the agent set the variable and invoke the script together in a single Bash tool call so the script inherits the variable in its execution environment.
Raise BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS so the exported environment variable remains available for longer between successive Bash commands.
Instruct the agent to issue the export in a Bash call immediately before the archival script call so the variable is still current when the script runs.

explanation: "The mental model to hold for the Bash built-in tool is that it is not a persistent shell session: each tool call runs its command separately, and exported environment variables do not survive across Bash tool calls. When an agent runs export CASE_ID=CS-88213 in one call and ./scripts/archive_case.sh in the next, the script starts without that variable in its environment.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.When the agent escalates a case, it must produce a self-contained handoff file at a fixed path (handoff-summary.md) containing the customer ID, root cause analysis, and recommended action. A previous escalation earlier in the same session may have already created this file, and the new summary must completely replace whatever is there so human agents never see stale details from an earlier case. The agent has already read the existing file during the current conversation. Which built-in tool usage should the agent apply?

choices.text: Call the Edit tool with the entire old summary as old_string and the entire new summary as new_string.
Call the Edit tool to update only the customer ID and recommended action fields, leaving the rest of the file unchanged.
Call the Write tool with the full new summary content targeting handoff-summary.md.
Call the Bash tool to echo the new summary into handoff-summary.md with shell output redirection.

explanation: "The built-in file tools divide responsibilities cleanly: Read loads contents, Edit makes targeted in-place changes via exact string replacement, and Write creates a file or completely overwrites an existing one with the full content you supply. The mental model is that Write is a full-file replacement operation, never a merge or append. When the goal is to fully regenerate a file, such as a structured escalation handoff that must never carry stale data forward, Write maps directly to the intent, whereas Edit maps to intent like fixing one field inside a document.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.To automate framework upgrade migrations, the team built a lightweight agentic loop directly against the Claude API, exposing a run_tests tool that executes the project's test suite. When the test command exits with a non-zero status, the harness currently swallows the failure and appends a tool_result containing only the text "done", after which Claude proceeds to finalize the migration. A review of recent branches shows several upgrades merged with failing tests that the agent never attempted to diagnose. What change to the loop's tool execution handling best enables the agent to recover from test failures autonomously?

choices.text: Return the test command's failure output in the tool_result block with is_error set to true so Claude can reason about the failure and adjust its approach.
Have the harness automatically re-run the failing test command with identical input up to three times before appending a success result.
Add a system prompt instruction requiring Claude to confirm that all tests passed before it finalizes any migration changes.
Terminate the loop immediately whenever the test tool returns a non-zero exit code and hand the branch back to a developer for manual investigation.

explanation: "An agentic loop works because Claude follows a reason, act, observe cycle: it decides on an action, your harness executes the corresponding tool, and the result is fed back as a tool_result that Claude observes before deciding what to do next. The model has no visibility into anything that happens outside its context window, so the fidelity of the loop depends entirely on what your code puts into each tool result. A harness that replaces a real failure with a generic success string severs the observation step; from Claude's perspective the tests passed, and its subsequent decision to finalize the migration is perfectly rational given the (false) evidence it was shown.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is a first-contact resolution rate of 80% or higher, with reliable escalation to a human when a case falls outside what the agent should handle.While prototyping the agent's control loop directly against the Claude API, a developer wrote code that, after executing each tool call, sends a fresh request containing only the system prompt, the customer's original message, and the latest tool result formatted as text. In testing, the agent calls get_customer successfully but then calls get_customer again on the next iteration with identical arguments, never progressing to lookup_order, until the iteration cap is reached. What change to the loop most directly fixes this behavior?

choices.text: Raise the loop's maximum iteration count so the agent has enough turns to eventually reach lookup_order after re-verifying the customer.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to remember which tools it has already called and never repeat a completed verification step.
Append each assistant tool_use response and its tool_result to the messages array, and resend the accumulated conversation history on every request.
Enable prompt caching with cache_control on the system prompt so the API retains the results of earlier tool calls between successive requests.

explanation: "The defining property of the Claude API is that it is stateless: there is no server-side memory between calls. Every request must carry the entire conversation in the messages array. The canonical agentic loop therefore does two things on every iteration: it appends the assistant message containing the tool_use block, then appends a user message containing the matching tool_result, and resends the whole accumulated history. When the developer's loop sends only the latest tool result as text, each request looks to Claude like the very first turn of the conversation, so it reasons from scratch and calls get_customer again; the loop is not broken because Claude is confused, but because the application layer erased its memory.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your custom MCP server exposes tools like lookup_service and file_ticket against your internal service catalog. During a code review of the server, you find a single catch-all handler that converts every failure into a CallToolResult with isError: true, covering four cases: the agent requesting a tool name the server does not define, timeouts from the upstream catalog API, service IDs that fail format validation, and requests for catalog entries the caller is not permitted to view. According to the Model Context Protocol specification, which change should you make to this handler?

choices.text: Report service IDs that fail input format validation through a JSON-RPC error response instead of a tool result.
Report requests for catalog entries the caller is not permitted to view through a JSON-RPC error response instead of a tool result.
Report requests that name a tool the server does not define through a JSON-RPC error response instead of a tool result.
Report timeouts from the upstream service catalog API through a JSON-RPC error response instead of a tool result.

explanation: "The Model Context Protocol defines two distinct error paths, and choosing the right one is a core part of tool interface design. Protocol errors cover problems with the request itself: unknown tool names, requests that fail the CallToolRequest schema, and server-level failures. These are reported through the standard JSON-RPC error object, which must include an integer code and a message, and a response must never carry both result and error. Tool execution errors cover failures that occur while running a valid tool call, including API failures, input validation errors, and business logic errors; these are reported inside a normal result with isError: true.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team is building an internal MCP server that exposes your issue tracker to Claude Code sessions. The initial design defines 16 separate tools (ticket_create, ticket_close, ticket_assign, ticket_comment, ticket_label_add, ticket_label_remove, and similar), each with a one-line description. During testing, Claude frequently invokes the wrong tool for a request or pauses to ask the developer which tool it should use. Which redesign most effectively improves tool selection reliability?

choices.text: Keep all 16 tools unchanged but add few-shot invocation examples to the project CLAUDE.md showing which tool to call for common request types.
Rename each of the 16 tools with longer, more descriptive and specific names while keeping the one-line descriptions and one-operation-per-tool structure.
Replace the 16 tools with a single dispatch tool that accepts a free-text instruction string and routes each request to the correct operation server-side.
Consolidate related operations into fewer tools with an enum-constrained action parameter, and write multi-sentence descriptions of when each applies.

explanation: Two design flaws compound in this MCP server: the tool surface is fragmented into many single-verb tools, and each tool carries a description too thin to differentiate it from its neighbors. Anthropic's guidance addresses both. Rather than one tool per verb, consolidate related operations into fewer, more capable tools, for example a ticket-management tool with an action parameter constrained by an enum (create, close, assign, comment). This shrinks the decision space Claude has to navigate on every turn while keeping inputs structured and validatable.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems. The extraction pipeline defines an extract_contract_terms tool whose input_schema includes effective_date, execution_date, and termination_date fields, each typed as a date-formatted string. Production logs show every model response is a tool call whose input parses and validates against the schema. However, QA sampling reveals that when a contract mentions several dates, the model frequently places the signing date in effective_date and the effective date in execution_date, corrupting downstream contract lifecycle tracking. Which change most directly addresses this misassignment?

choices.text: Add top-level strict: true to the tool definition so the model's tool inputs are constrained to conform to the JSON Schema during sampling.
Set tool_choice to force the extract_contract_terms tool so that every response is guaranteed to be a call to that specific tool.
Mark all three date fields as required in the input_schema so the model must populate every one of them on each extraction.
Add a description to each date field in the input_schema defining what that field represents and how it differs from the other dates.

explanation: "The failure in this pipeline is semantic, not syntactic. Tool use with JSON schemas is highly reliable at producing well-formed, schema-conformant output, but the schema is a structural contract: it says a field named effective_date must contain a date-formatted string, not which date from the document that should be. When two fields are semantically adjacent (signing date versus effective date), the model must infer the distinction from whatever guidance the schema and prompt provide. If the fields carry only names and types, that inference is fragile.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.The extraction pipeline currently runs as a single Agent SDK session that processes a batch of lengthy vendor contracts one after another, reading each contract's full text and reasoning through the extraction before moving to the next. Quality audits show that accuracy is high for the first few contracts but degrades later in the batch, and by the tenth contract the structured output sometimes contains party names and payment terms that actually belong to earlier contracts. Which architectural change most directly addresses this problem?

choices.text: Restructure the session as a coordinator that delegates each contract to an extraction subagent spawned with its own fresh isolated context.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to completely disregard all previously processed contracts when extracting from a new document.
Raise the maximum output token limit so each extraction response has room to include more complete and detailed field values.
Enable extended thinking for each extraction so the agent reasons more carefully about which contract each field value belongs to.

explanation: "This failure pattern is a classic consequence of context accumulation in a single long-running agent session. Every contract's full text, plus the intermediate reasoning about it, remains in the context window as the batch progresses. Later extractions therefore operate against a window crowded with irrelevant earlier material, and the model's attention can bleed values from one document into another. No amount of instruction can fix this, because the problem is structural: the contaminating tokens are physically present in every subsequent request.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.The system's coordinator agent, built with the Claude Agent SDK, processes regulatory filings that each contain three independent sections: financial tables, risk disclosures, and exhibit lists. A section-extractor subagent (defined via the agents parameter) extracts structured JSON from a single section. Currently the coordinator delegates one section, waits for that subagent's result, then spawns the next subagent in a later turn, so total processing time is roughly the sum of all three extractions. The sections have no dependencies on each other. What change would most effectively reduce end-to-end processing time for each filing?

choices.text: Remove the subagent delegation entirely and have the coordinator read and extract all three sections directly in the main conversation to avoid spawn overhead.
Include the coordinator's full conversation history in each subagent's delegation prompt so extractors can reuse earlier findings and finish faster.
Have the coordinator spawn a section-extractor subagent for each of the three sections concurrently in a single turn, then aggregate their results.
Restructure the subagents into a pipeline where each section extractor passes its output into the next extractor's prompt so results flow through the chain.

explanation: "Subagents in the Claude Agent SDK exist to make exactly this tradeoff: each one runs in its own isolated context window, does its verbose work there, and returns only a final result to the parent. Two properties follow from that design. First, intermediate content (raw document text, tool results) never accumulates in the coordinator's context. Second, because each subagent is an independent conversation, multiple subagents can run concurrently, so a set of independent subtasks completes in roughly the time of the slowest one rather than the sum of all of them. When a coordinator has genuinely independent work items, like three unrelated sections of a filing, spawning the extractors in the same turn and aggregating their structured outputs is the intended pattern.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.The team's pipeline currently extracts a 45-field schema (parties, payment terms, liability caps, termination conditions, renewal clauses) from 150-page vendor contracts using a single extraction call over the full document. Validation logs show a consistent pattern: fields whose source clauses appear in the middle of the contract are frequently null or incorrect, while fields drawn from the opening and closing sections are reliably accurate. How should the extraction task be redesigned to address this?

choices.text: Enable extended thinking on the single full-document extraction pass so the model reasons more deliberately about each clause before emitting the extracted fields.
Keep the single full-document extraction pass but mark all 45 fields as required and remove null from their type definitions so the schema no longer permits null values for mid-document fields.
Add a validation-retry loop that resends the full contract with the complete 45-field schema and the specific validation errors whenever mid-document fields come back null or incorrect.
Split the extraction into focused passes, each targeting a related subset of fields against the relevant contract sections, then merge results with a cross-field consistency check.

explanation: "The diagnostic signal in this scenario is positional: fields sourced from the beginning and end of the contract extract accurately, while fields sourced from the middle degrade. That is the signature of the lost-in-the-middle effect, where information in the middle of a long context receives less attention than information at the edges, compounded by attention dilution when a single pass must satisfy a broad 45-field schema against 150 pages at once. No amount of retrying, schema tightening, or extra reasoning changes where the model's attention falls within one enormous input.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.To produce structured output, the team defines an extract_invoice tool whose input_schema mirrors the target record and forces it on every call with tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}. The schema declares invoice_date and currency as plain string fields with no field-level descriptions. Every response is syntactically valid JSON, but invoice_date arrives inconsistently as "03/31/2026", "March 31, 2026", or "2026-03-31", and currency appears variously as "USD", "$", and "US Dollars", causing the downstream billing system to reject records. What is the highest-leverage change to the tool interface?

choices.text: Build a retry loop that resends the full document with the validation error whenever the billing system rejects a record's formatting.
Add field descriptions specifying the exact expected format for invoice_date and constrain currency with an enum of accepted codes.
Change tool_choice from the named tool to "any" so Claude has more flexibility in how it structures the extraction call.
Rename the fields to invoice_date_iso8601 and currency_code so the field names themselves convey the expected formats.

explanation: "Defining a tool whose input_schema matches your target record is the most reliable route to structured output, but it is important to understand exactly what the schema enforces. Claude is trained to emit valid JSON matching the schema's shape: braces close, declared types are respected, required fields are present. A plain "type": "string" field, however, says nothing about which of many equally valid string renderings the model should choose, so dates and currency labels drift across calls.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.During QA review of a report the system produced on global solar capacity growth, a reviewer notices that the final report states a single capacity figure as established fact. Inspecting the web search subagent's raw output, they find two credible sources with materially different figures, published two years apart. The summaries the synthesis agent received were prose paragraphs containing neither source names nor publication dates, and the synthesis agent silently included only one of the two figures. What change most effectively addresses this failure?

choices.text: Restrict the web search subagent to a curated allowlist containing one authoritative source per topic so conflicting statistics never enter the pipeline.
Require subagents to emit structured claim-source records with publication dates, and have the synthesis agent surface conflicting figures with attribution.
Add an independent review instance that re-checks the report and replaces any disputed statistic with the value that appears in the majority of sources.
Instruct the synthesis agent to resolve statistical conflicts automatically by always adopting the figure from the most recently published source.

explanation: "The root failure here is that source attribution was lost during summarization: once findings were compressed into prose without source names or dates, the synthesis agent had no way to recognize that two figures came from different sources published at different times, so it silently picked one. The fix must operate on the data contract between agents, not on the synthesis agent's judgment alone. Requiring each subagent to emit claim-source mappings (claim, evidence excerpt, source identifier, publication date) as structured output means provenance survives every downstream combination step, and the synthesis agent can be instructed to annotate conflicts with attribution instead of resolving them unilaterally.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.During pilot runs, the synthesis subagent frequently encounters small factual questions (publication dates, correct spellings of researcher names, whether a cited statistic matches its source) and must pause and ask the coordinator to re-delegate each one to the web search subagent. This round-tripping adds significant latency and fills the coordinator's context with trivial delegation traffic, while deeper follow-up research genuinely does need the search subagent's full capabilities. How should you adjust the tool distribution to fix this?

choices.text: Have the coordinator pre-emptively spawn several parallel search subagents alongside every synthesis task to answer verification questions as they arise.
Give the synthesis subagent a scoped fact-verification lookup tool, routing complex follow-up research through the coordinator to the search subagent.
Update the synthesis subagent's system prompt to mark unverified facts with an explicit caveat in the report instead of attempting any verification.
Give the synthesis subagent the search subagent's complete web search and page-fetching toolset so it never needs to delegate any verification work.

explanation: "The core tension in tool distribution across a multi-agent system is between scoped tool access (each subagent gets only the tools its role needs, keeping tool selection reliable and roles clean) and the practical reality that some needs cross role boundaries. The design pattern for that tension is the limited cross-role tool: when one agent has a high-frequency but low-complexity need that formally belongs to another agent's role, give it a narrow, purpose-built tool for exactly that need, while continuing to route the complex cases through the coordinator to the specialist.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.A developer platform team runs a nightly job that generates plain-language explanations of legacy modules for the internal developer portal. Each night it submits about 20,000 requests in a single Message Batches API batch, then a downstream script attaches the Nth result line to the Nth submitted module. Recently some explanations have appeared under the wrong modules, and on a few nights a handful of requests came back with an expired result type, leaving those modules blank. Which change most effectively makes the pipeline reliable while preserving the batch cost savings?

choices.text: Replace the batch with 20,000 sequential synchronous Messages API calls overnight so each response can be paired with its request immediately.
Assign each request a unique custom_id derived from its module, join results to modules on custom_id, and resubmit only requests whose result type is errored or expired in a follow-up batch.
Cancel the batch whenever any request returns an error, discard any partial results, and resubmit all 20,000 requests as a fresh batch.
Poll the batch until its processing_status becomes ended, then rely on the JSONL result order matching submission order, rerunning the entire batch on any night when a request expires.

explanation: "The Message Batches API treats each item in a batch as an independent Messages request, and it makes no promise about the order in which results appear: the results file is JSONL that may be returned in any order. That is why every request must carry a unique custom_id (1 to 64 characters matching ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$); it is the only reliable join key between the rows you submitted and the rows you get back. A pipeline that matches by position will work often enough to pass a quick test and then silently misattribute results in production, which is exactly the failure the portal team observed.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.The extraction pipeline submits each extracted record to the downstream database through a custom MCP tool, submit_record, which validates the payload against the downstream JSON schema before ingestion. Production logs reveal two distinct failure patterns: records with dates formatted as MM/DD/YYYY instead of the required ISO 8601 format, and records missing a required invoice_number because the source document never contained one. In both cases, submit_record returns a tool result with isError: true and the message "Schema validation failed". Claude retries both cases identically, never correcting the date format, and on missing-field records it eventually fabricates a plausible invoice number to satisfy the schema. What change to the tool's error responses would most improve reliability?

choices.text: Keep the current error message unchanged but add a system prompt instruction that limits the agent to two retry attempts per record before it skips to the next source document.

Capping retries limits wasted effort but gives the agent no information about what went wrong or how to fix it. Format errors that the agent could correct with the right feedback would still fail and be skipped, and the underlying incentive to fabricate values for missing fields is not addressed.
Return the validation failures with isError set to false so the agent treats them as normal results and stops retrying, then filter out the failed records downstream.

Convert the schema validation failures into JSON-RPC error responses with distinct integer error codes so the client application can differentiate the two failure types programmatically. E Return categorized error metadata that marks format violations as retryable with the expected format and missing source data as non-retryable, directing the record to human review. Answer: E Explanation. "The Model Context Protocol distinguishes protocol errors (unknown tools, malformed requests), which use the JSON-RPC error object, from tool execution errors (validation failures, business logic failures), which are reported inside a normal result with isError: true. The spec's rationale is that execution errors should carry actionable feedback the model can use to self-correct, and clients SHOULD surface them to the model, whereas protocol errors only MAY be surfaced because they rarely lead to recovery. A bare message like 'Schema validation failed' technically follows the pattern but defeats its purpose: the agent knows something failed but not what to do next.

explanation: "The Model Context Protocol distinguishes protocol errors (unknown tools, malformed requests), which use the JSON-RPC error object, from tool execution errors (validation failures, business logic failures), which are reported inside a normal result with isError: true. The spec's rationale is that execution errors should carry actionable feedback the model can use to self-correct, and clients SHOULD surface them to the model, whereas protocol errors only MAY be surfaced because they rarely lead to recovery. A bare message like 'Schema validation failed' technically follows the pattern but defeats its purpose: the agent knows something failed but not what to do next.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The report-generation subagent in this system has access to a distribute_report tool exposed by a custom MCP server named reports (surfaced to the agent as mcp__reports__distribute_report) that emails finished reports to an external subscriber list, an action that cannot be recalled once sent. Compliance policy requires a human reviewer to approve every report before it is distributed. The coordinator's system prompt instructs the agent to wait for approval before calling the tool, yet audit logs show two reports were emailed without any approval step occurring. Which change most reliably enforces the approval requirement?

choices.text: Add a PreToolUse hook whose matcher targets mcp__reports__distribute_report and returns a permissionDecision of ask so a human must approve each call before it executes.
Add a Stop hook that blocks the agent from ending its turn until it verifies an approval record exists for every report it has distributed.
Expand the system prompt with few-shot examples showing the agent pausing and requesting human approval before each distribution call.
Add a PostToolUse hook matching mcp__reports__distribute_report that checks whether an approval record exists and feeds an error back to the agent when it does not.

explanation: "The core distinction here is between pre-execution enforcement and post-execution feedback. Only a PreToolUse hook (or an equivalent ask rule that routes to a permission callback) intercepts a tool call before it runs, which is the only point in the loop where an irreversible action like emailing an external subscriber list can still be stopped. Returning a permissionDecision of ask converts the call into an explicit human approval gate, turning a probabilistic prompt instruction into a deterministic control that fires on every invocation, including runs no one is watching. One practical detail matters: MCP tools are surfaced under names of the form mcp____, so the hook matcher must target mcp__reports__distribute_report (or an anchored pattern matching that full name), not the bare tool name.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team wrote a script that uses Claude to generate documentation metadata for legacy modules: for each source file, the prompt describes a JSON format (function name, parameters, return type, summary) and asks Claude to return matching JSON. A validation step checks each response against a JSON schema, and on failure the retry loop resends the exact same request, up to three times. Logs show that when a response fails validation (for example, a missing required parameters field or a type mismatch on return type), the retries almost always fail with the identical error until the budget is exhausted. Which change to the retry loop most effectively improves extraction reliability?

choices.text: Add an assistant prefill that starts the response with an opening brace so the output is guaranteed to begin as JSON.
Relax the JSON schema by making the frequently failing fields optional so fewer responses are rejected by validation.
Change the retry request to include the original source file, the failed output, and the specific validation error so the model can correct the identified problem.
Increase the retry limit from three attempts to eight so the model has more opportunities to produce a schema-compliant response.

explanation: "A validation-retry loop is only as good as the feedback it carries. The mental model is a conversation, not a slot machine: Claude generates output, your code validates it against the schema, and when validation fails, the retry should send back the original input, the failed output, and the specific validation error. Given that context, the model can locate and fix the exact structural problem (add the missing parameters field, correct the type of return_type). Resending an identical request provides no new information, so the model tends to make the same mistake again, which is exactly the pattern the logs show; raising the retry ceiling just repeats that failure more times at higher cost.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.The extraction pipeline embeds the Claude Agent SDK, and an invoice-extractor subagent handles per-document field extraction. A developer updates the invoice-extractor definition in the repository's .claude/agents/invoice-extractor.md file with new rules for handling missing tax fields, but production runs continue to extract using the old behavior. Reviewing the application code, you find that the pipeline also passes an "invoice-extractor" AgentDefinition through the agents parameter in query() options, containing the original system prompt. What change will make the new field-handling rules take effect?

choices.text: Move the markdown file from .claude/agents/ to ~/.claude/agents/ so the updated definition loads from a higher-priority location.
Add an instruction in the coordinator's prompt to explicitly say "use the invoice-extractor agent" so the filesystem definition is invoked directly.
Restart the extraction service so a fresh session re-reads the .claude/agents/ directory, since agent files are only discovered at session start.
Update the AgentDefinition passed through the agents parameter in query() options so it contains the new field-handling rules.

explanation: "Subagent definitions in the Claude Agent SDK can come from several sources at once: the agents parameter in query() options, project-level files in .claude/agents/, user-level files in ~/.claude/agents/, and plugin directories. When two sources define an agent with the same name, resolution follows a fixed precedence: programmatic definitions override filesystem-based agents with the same name, and among filesystem scopes, project files outrank user files. This is why editing the markdown file had no visible effect; the SDK application was silently shadowing it with the original AgentDefinition, and updating that programmatic definition is what makes the new rules take effect.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.The extraction pipeline uses tool_use with a JSON schema in which optional fields like purchase order number and vendor tax ID are nullable, and the prompt explicitly instructs Claude to return null when a field is absent from the document. The prompt also includes three few-shot examples, all drawn from complete invoices where every output field is populated. In production, when an invoice omits the purchase order number, Claude frequently outputs a plausible-looking fabricated value instead of null; the resulting JSON always passes schema validation. What change would most effectively eliminate this fabrication?

choices.text: Enable strict tool use on the extraction tool definition so Claude's tool inputs are validated against the schema.
Implement a validation-retry loop that sends schema validation errors back to Claude for self-correction.
Rewrite the prompt instruction to state more forcefully that fabricating values is prohibited and null is required for absent fields.
Add few-shot examples of documents with missing fields whose corresponding output shows null for those fields.

explanation: "Few-shot examples do not just illustrate format; Claude treats them as evidence of the expected pattern, and that inferred pattern can override explicit written instructions when the two conflict. Here every example shows a fully populated output, so the examples silently teach that all fields always have values. When the source document lacks a purchase order number, the model resolves the tension between the null instruction and the all-populated examples in favor of the examples, fabricating a plausible value. Anthropic's guidance is direct about this failure mode: examples should mirror the real use case and cover edge cases, otherwise Claude may infer unintended patterns from them.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.The team's agent integrates a custom MCP tool, query_code_index, that performs read-only lookups against an internal code search index. During codebase exploration sessions, Claude frequently requests several Read and Grep calls together with multiple query_code_index calls in a single turn. Logs show the built-in Read and Grep calls execute concurrently, but the query_code_index calls always execute one at a time, noticeably slowing exploration. What change would allow the custom tool's calls to run concurrently within a turn?

choices.text: Set the readOnlyHint annotation on the query_code_index tool definition so the SDK can schedule its calls concurrently.
Switch the session's permission mode to acceptEdits so the SDK stops enforcing sequential ordering for the tool's calls.
Add mcp__code_index__* to the session's allowedTools list so calls to the tool are auto-approved without prompting.
Update the system prompt to instruct Claude to issue all query_code_index calls in parallel within a single response.

explanation: "When Claude requests multiple tools in a single turn, the Agent SDK does not treat all of them the same way. Built-in read-only tools such as Read, Glob, and Grep, along with MCP tools known to be read-only, can execute concurrently, while state-changing tools like Edit, Write, and Bash run sequentially to avoid conflicting side effects. Custom tools default to sequential execution because the SDK cannot know whether they mutate state; the readOnlyHint annotation is how a tool author declares that a tool is safe to parallelize.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team adds a PreToolUse hook to prevent Claude from running database-reset commands during refactoring sessions. The hook script correctly detects the dangerous command, prints a warning message to stderr, and exits with code 1. During testing, the warning appears in the session logs, but Claude still executes the database-reset command every time. What change most reliably enforces the block?

choices.text: Change the hook script to exit with code 2 so the tool call is blocked and the stderr message is fed back to Claude.
Print the warning message to stdout instead of stderr so Claude Code can parse the hook's output and stop the call.
Add an explicit rule to CLAUDE.md stating that database-reset commands must never be executed during refactoring work.
Move the enforcement logic to a PostToolUse hook so it can inspect and reject the command after Claude issues it.

explanation: "Claude Code hooks communicate their outcome to the agent loop through a small, deterministic protocol: a hook that does not return structured JSON signals its decision with its exit code. Exit code 0 means success (any JSON on stdout is parsed as a decision). Exit code 2 means a blocking error: the tool call is stopped, and whatever the hook wrote to stderr is injected back into Claude's context so the model understands why it was blocked and can choose a different approach. Every other non-zero exit code, including 1, is treated as a non-blocking failure that is merely logged, and Claude proceeds to run the tool anyway. This is a common trap because 1 is the conventional Unix failure code, so it feels like it should block; in the hook protocol it does not.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.This team's monorepo has a root CLAUDE.md mandating TypeScript strict mode with Zod validation for all new code. One package, packages/legacy-scheduler/, is plain JavaScript and cannot adopt those standards, so the team added a packages/legacy-scheduler/CLAUDE.md stating "Ignore the root TypeScript standards; this package uses plain JavaScript without Zod," expecting it to replace the root instructions when engineers launch Claude Code from that directory. Engineers working in that package report that Claude Code still inconsistently proposes converting files to TypeScript and adding Zod schemas. What change most reliably fixes this behavior?

choices.text: Reword the root CLAUDE.md so the TypeScript strict mode and Zod rules explicitly exempt packages/legacy-scheduler/, eliminating the contradiction between the two files.
Move the exception into a CLAUDE.local.md file inside packages/legacy-scheduler/ so it is appended after the other files and takes precedence over them.
Instruct engineers to launch Claude Code from the repository root so the package-level CLAUDE.md is not loaded and the conflict never enters context.
Copy the root CLAUDE.md into packages/legacy-scheduler/ with the TypeScript rules removed, so the file closer to the working directory replaces the root file for that package.

explanation: "The essential mental model is that the CLAUDE.md hierarchy is additive. When Claude Code starts, it walks up the directory tree from the working directory and loads every discovered CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md, concatenating them from the filesystem root down to where the session was launched. Nothing in this mechanism replaces or overrides anything else; a package-level file does not shadow the root file, it simply appears later in the same context. Anthropic designed it this way so broad team conventions and local specifics compose, with each level adding detail rather than forcing teams to re-declare everything at every depth.
