stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.To generate large boilerplate modules, the team prototyped a custom agentic loop directly against the Claude API. The loop sends the messages array with tools, executes tool calls while stop_reason is "tool_use", and treats any other stop_reason as completion, writing the final text response to a file. Occasionally the generated files end abruptly mid-function, and logs show those runs ended with a stop_reason of "max_tokens". What change to the loop most directly fixes this failure?

choices.text: Raise the loop's maximum iteration safety cap so the agent has more opportunities to finish generating the module before the loop is forced to stop.
Handle the "max_tokens" stop reason as a truncation case, raising the output token limit or continuing the generation, instead of treating every non-tool_use response as a completed result.
Run a syntax check on the final output and, whenever it fails, discard the attempt and restart the entire request from scratch with the same parameters.

Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to keep each response within the token limit and to end every completed module with a distinctive END marker, then terminate the loop only when the marker is present.

explanation: "Every Claude API response carries a stop_reason that tells your loop why generation halted, and robust agentic loops must distinguish all of its values rather than collapsing them into a binary continue-or-done check. tool_use means Claude wants a tool executed, so the loop continues; end_turn means Claude genuinely finished; but max_tokens means the output token cap was hit and the response is truncated, not complete. A loop written as 'anything other than tool_use means done' will happily write half-generated code to disk, which is exactly the failure the logs reveal here.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team's shared .mcp.json registers a custom MCP server exposing a get_table_schema tool that queries the development database so Claude Code can generate data-access code that matches your schema. Reviewing the server code, you find that when the database is unreachable, the handler catches the exception and returns a normal tool result whose content is the text "ERROR: connection refused", with the isError field left unset. Session transcripts show Claude Code sometimes treats that text as if it were schema output and generates model classes from faulty assumptions, and other times proceeds without acknowledging the failure. What change to the server's error handling best addresses this?

choices.text: Add an instruction to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to treat any tool output beginning with "ERROR:" as a failure and stop generating code.
Return the failure in the tool result with isError set to true and a descriptive message indicating the database connection failed and the call can be retried.
Return an empty content array on connection failures so Claude detects the failure from the absence of schema data.
Convert the connection failure into a JSON-RPC error response with an integer error code so the failure surfaces at the protocol level.

explanation: "The Model Context Protocol draws a sharp line between two kinds of failures. Protocol errors, such as calling an unknown tool or sending a malformed request, are reported as standard JSON-RPC error objects with an integer code and message. Tool execution errors, such as upstream API failures, connectivity problems, or business logic failures, are reported inside a normal tool result with isError: true. The reason for this design is agent recovery: the spec states that execution errors should contain actionable feedback the model can use to self-correct, and that clients SHOULD deliver execution errors to the model while they only MAY deliver protocol errors, which are less likely to lead to recovery.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.One engineer on this team runs a local mock of the web-search subagent's external API for offline development. They want Claude Code to point generated code at the mock endpoint and add extra debug logging conventions, but only in their own sessions within this repository. Teammates pulling the repo must not receive these instructions, and the engineer's other repositories must be unaffected. Where should these instructions live?

choices.text: In a CLAUDE.local.md file at the repository root, added to .gitignore.
In a .claude/rules/ file with a paths frontmatter scoped to the search subagent's directory.
In the ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file on the engineer's machine.
In the project's root CLAUDE.md, under a section header labeled with the engineer's name.

explanation: "Claude Code loads memory files from several distinct scopes, and choosing the right one comes down to two axes: who should receive the instructions and where they should apply. The project CLAUDE.md is team-and-repo scoped (shared via version control), ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is user-and-everywhere scoped (private but loaded in every project), and CLAUDE.local.md fills the remaining quadrant: user-and-repo scoped. It sits at the project root, is appended after the project CLAUDE.md during loading, and is meant to be gitignored so it never propagates to teammates.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The web search subagent in this system calls an MCP search tool that returns 40+ fields per result, including raw HTML bodies and crawl metadata, although downstream agents only ever use the title, URL, snippet, and publication date. During long research runs, these verbose payloads fill the web search subagent's context window and its later reasoning quality degrades. Which hook-based design deterministically ensures only the relevant fields enter the agent's context?

choices.text: Add instructions to the web search subagent's system prompt telling it to disregard all fields except title, URL, snippet, and publication date.
Register a PostToolUseFailure hook matching the MCP search tool that truncates oversized search responses before Claude processes the results.
Register a PostToolUse hook matching the MCP search tool that returns updatedToolOutput with only the title, URL, snippet, and publication date.
Register a PreToolUse hook matching the MCP search tool that returns updatedInput to filter the search response down to the four needed fields.

explanation: "The Agent SDK exposes distinct hook events on either side of tool execution, and choosing the right one depends on what you need to transform. PreToolUse runs after Claude has drafted the tool parameters but before the call is processed, so its updatedInput field can rewrite what goes into the tool. PostToolUse runs after a tool succeeds and receives both tool_input and tool_response; returning updatedToolOutput replaces the result the model actually sees. Because tool results accumulate in the conversation and consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance, trimming a 40+ field payload down to the four fields that matter is one of the highest-leverage context-management moves in an agentic system.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.This team stores its extraction JSON schemas and prompt templates in a GitHub repository and has added the anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 workflow in automation mode to review every pull request that modifies a schema. The workflow's permissions block grants contents: read, pull-requests: write, and issues: write. Every run fails at startup with an error indicating the action could not obtain a GitHub App token, before Claude performs any review. The ANTHROPIC_API_KEY secret has been verified as valid. What change should the team make?

choices.text: Replace the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY secret with a CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN generated via claude setup-token.
Add actions: read to the workflow's permissions block.
Change contents: read to contents: write in the workflow's permissions block.
Add id-token: write to the workflow's permissions block.

explanation: "GitHub Actions workflows operate under an explicit permissions block, and anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 depends on one permission that is easy to overlook: id-token: write. This permission does not grant Claude any repository capability directly; it allows the workflow to mint an OpenID Connect (OIDC) token, which the action exchanges for a short-lived GitHub App token under its default authentication flow. That exchange happens at startup, before any prompt is processed, which is why a missing id-token: write produces an authentication failure before Claude ever begins the review. The design tradeoff is deliberate: OIDC-based exchange avoids storing long-lived GitHub credentials as secrets, at the cost of requiring this extra permission grant.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.Your team uses Claude Code to iteratively refine the extraction prompt for this system. Each time a new document edge case fails (for example, invoices with line items in multiple currencies), an engineer describes the failure to Claude, Claude revises the prompt, and the new case starts extracting correctly. However, later spot-checks keep revealing that document types which previously extracted correctly now produce schema-invalid or incorrect JSON. Which refinement approach would most effectively enable progressive improvement without these regressions?

choices.text: Enter plan mode before each refinement so Claude proposes and explains the prompt change for your review and approval before applying it to the system.
Build a fixture set of documents with expected JSON outputs, and have Claude run schema validation across the full set after each revision, fixing any diffs.
Append a prose rule for each new edge case to the extraction prompt and ask Claude to confirm that the revised prompt still handles every previously reported case.
Use /rewind to restore the checkpoint from before the most recent regression appeared, then re-apply the latest prompt change on top of the restored state.

explanation: "The failure pattern here is classic regression during iterative refinement: each fix is validated only against the case that prompted it, so nothing measures whether earlier cases still work. Anthropic's guidance for progressive improvement is to ground iteration in a verifiable check Claude can run itself, such as tests, schema validators, or fixture diffs, so Claude can read concrete results and keep iterating until everything passes rather than declaring success based on how the output looks. For an extraction system, a fixture set of documents paired with gold-standard JSON outputs turns every prompt revision into a measurable experiment: run the extraction across the whole set, validate against the JSON schema, diff against the expected outputs, and feed the failures back into the next iteration.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.Your extraction pipeline processes three document types (invoices, purchase orders, and shipping manifests), each handled by a separate extraction tool with its own input_schema, and the document type is not known before the API call. In production, about 8% of requests come back as a plain text block in which Claude summarizes the document or asks a clarifying question instead of invoking any extraction tool, which breaks the downstream parser that expects a tool call on every request. Which tool_choice configuration best guarantees a tool call on every request while still letting Claude pick the schema that matches the document?

choices.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "none"} and instruct Claude to emit JSON in its text response that matches the appropriate schema.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"} so every request is guaranteed to produce a tool call.
Keep tool_choice as auto and add an explicit system prompt instruction that Claude must always call exactly one extraction tool.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so Claude must invoke one of the provided extraction tools on every response.

explanation: "The tool_choice parameter accepts four values: auto (Claude decides whether to use a tool; the default when tools are supplied), any (Claude must use one of the available tools but chooses which), tool (a specific named tool is forced), and none (no tool use). The mental model is a dial of increasing constraint: auto preserves the option of a text answer, any removes the text-only escape hatch while preserving tool selection, and tool removes selection as well. When the failure mode is 'the model sometimes answers in prose instead of calling a tool' and multiple schemas must remain selectable, any is the precise fit; when a particular extraction must run, such as forcing metadata extraction before enrichment, the named tool form is the right dial position instead.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your team's agent uses a canUseTool callback to route risky Bash commands (such as force pushes and recursive deletes) to a senior engineer for approval before execution. To reduce interruptions, the agent's configuration also includes permission allow rules that pre-approve several common Bash command patterns. An audit reveals that some risky commands matching those pre-approved patterns executed without the callback ever firing. Which change ensures every Bash command is evaluated by the human-review check?

choices.text: Switch the permission mode to default so every Bash command is routed to the canUseTool callback for approval.
Move the review logic into a PreToolUse hook, which runs before permission rules and modes are evaluated.

PreToolUse hooks execute before the rest of the permission flow, including allow rules and permission modes, so they see every tool call. This is the documented mechanism for checks that must apply universally, unlike the canUseTool callback, which is skipped for calls already approved earlier in the evaluation flow.

Add explicit system prompt instructions requiring the agent to pause and request confirmation before running destructive commands. E Add Bash to the allowed_tools list so its calls are guaranteed to reach the canUseTool callback.

explanation: "The Agent SDK evaluates permissions through a documented flow in which hooks run first, before permission rules and modes, and the canUseTool callback is consulted only for tool calls that were not already resolved earlier in the flow. The mental model is a series of gates: as soon as one stage resolves a tool call (for example, an allow rule pre-approving a matching Bash pattern), later stages never run. This is why the audit shows risky commands slipping past the callback; they matched the pre-approved patterns and the permission flow finished before canUseTool was ever consulted.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team asked Claude Code to generate architecture documentation for a legacy job scheduler's retry and error-handling behavior. During review, senior engineers found that several sections confidently describe configuration options and fallback paths that do not exist anywhere in the repository; Claude appears to have described common patterns for the underlying framework rather than the actual implementation. What change to the documentation workflow most effectively prevents these fabricated claims?

choices.text: Have a second Claude Code session without the original conversation context independently review the finished documentation for plausibility and internal consistency.
Add a CLAUDE.md rule stating that documentation must be strictly accurate and instructing Claude to double-check every section against the codebase before finalizing.
Have the workflow collect verbatim code excerpts with file paths first, generate sections only from those excerpts, and flag claims lacking a supporting excerpt as unverified.
Run the documentation task in plan mode so Claude explores the scheduler's code thoroughly before writing, then review and approve the plan and switch to direct execution.

explanation: "This failure is a classic grounding problem: when asked to document behavior it has not fully retrieved, a language model fills gaps with statistically typical patterns for the framework, stated with the same confidence as verified facts. The documented remedy is a quote-first workflow: extract verbatim excerpts (with file paths) from the source material, generate claims only from those excerpts, and treat any claim that cannot be tied to an excerpt as unverified or retract it. Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations recommends exactly this: ground long-document tasks by extracting direct quotes first, require citations for claims, allow the model to say it does not know, and drop claims that lack supporting evidence.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your agent generates codebase exploration reports that engineers use before modifying legacy systems. The system prompt contains three complete example reports wrapped in tags, and report structure is now highly consistent. Last month you added a written instruction requiring every report to end with a "Risks and Unknowns" section, but the three example reports predate this instruction and none of them contain that section. In production, the agent omits the "Risks and Unknowns" section in roughly 70% of reports while following the example structure faithfully. What change would most effectively fix this?

choices.text: Remove the few-shot examples entirely so the agent relies only on the detailed written instructions for report structure.
Add two more example reports in the current format to further reinforce the agent's structural consistency.
Update each few-shot example report to include a "Risks and Unknowns" section so the examples demonstrate the same structure the instructions require.
Rewrite the instruction with stronger emphasis (for example, "You MUST always include a Risks and Unknowns section") and move it to the top of the system prompt.

explanation: "The useful mental model here is that few-shot examples function as an implicit specification: Claude infers format, tone, and structure from what the examples actually show, and this signal is typically stronger than abstract written rules. Anthropic's guidance is explicit that examples should mirror the real use case closely, because Claude will pick up unintended patterns from them, and that demonstrating the desired output is more effective than describing it. When an instruction says one thing and every example demonstrates another, the model has two conflicting specifications, and the demonstrated pattern usually wins; the observed 70% omission rate is a symptom of this conflict, not of weak instruction wording.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Engineers on your team use the agent to remove dead code from legacy services as part of routine cleanup. Last month the agent used Grep to search for references to a handler function, found none, deleted it, and broke a nightly job because the handler was invoked through a method name assembled from strings at runtime. The legacy services also have sparse test coverage. You want the agent to keep removing clearly dead code autonomously while reliably pausing for human input on removals that are genuinely ambiguous. Which design best achieves this?

choices.text: Require the engineer to review and approve every individual deletion the agent proposes across each cleanup task.

Add explicit escalation criteria to the agent's instructions (string-based references, reflection, config-driven entry points) with few-shot examples, and have it surface matching candidates to the engineer instead of deleting them.
Instruct the agent to run the test suite after each removal and revert automatically whenever a test fails, treating a passing run as approval to continue.
Have the agent attach a self-reported confidence score to each proposed removal and automatically delete any candidate that scores above a high threshold.

explanation: "The core of this problem is ambiguity resolution design: deciding which situations an agent may resolve autonomously and which it must hand to a human. The failure in the stem is not that the agent lacked diligence; it followed a reasonable procedure (Grep for references, delete if none) that is simply blind to dynamic invocation, where call sites are constructed from strings, reflection, or configuration at runtime. No amount of general caution fixes a blind spot the agent cannot recognize; you have to name the blind spot explicitly.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.Your agent frequently generates shell scripts and boilerplate service code that engineers then run in their own environments. Before any generated artifact is written to disk, you already route it through an independent reviewer instance that has no access to the generator's conversation. Audits show the reviewer's findings vary run to run: one review catches a command injection risk but misses hardcoded credentials, another catches the credentials but misses unsafe file permissions, and no single pass reliably covers all vulnerability categories. Which architectural change would most effectively improve detection coverage?

choices.text: Ask the reviewer to output a confidence score per vulnerability category and rerun the review whenever a category's confidence falls below a threshold.
Run several reviewer instances in parallel, each prompted to check a different vulnerability category, and flag the artifact if any instance reports an issue.
Have the same reviewer instance perform a second review pass within the same conversation to catch issues it missed initially.
Enable extended thinking on the single reviewer instance so it reasons more deeply about all vulnerability categories in one pass.

explanation: "When a single review pass must simultaneously watch for injection, secrets, permissions, and other concerns, its attention is spread thin, and which category it catches becomes probabilistic from run to run. Anthropic's agentic workflow guidance documents parallelization as the remedy, in two forms: sectioning (splitting a task into independent subtasks run in parallel) and voting (running the same task multiple times to get diverse outputs). The canonical voting example is exactly this situation: reviewing code for vulnerabilities with several different prompts, where the code is flagged if any reviewer finds a problem. Each focused instance dedicates its full attention to one category, so aggregate coverage no longer depends on one pass noticing everything at once.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.During a research run on a pharmaceutical policy topic, the coordinator delegates four document sources to the document analysis subagent. One source is behind a paywall the subagent cannot access, and it reports this failure back to the coordinator. The coordinator's current behavior is to terminate the entire workflow and return "research failed" to the user, discarding the completed web search results and the three successfully analyzed documents. Which error propagation redesign best improves the system's resilience?

choices.text: Have the coordinator proceed with the successful subagents' findings and instruct the synthesis agent to annotate a coverage gap for the inaccessible source.
Configure the coordinator to restart the research workflow from the beginning, re-running all subagents whenever any single subagent reports a failure.
Route the run to a human reviewer whenever any subagent reports an error, pausing report generation until the reviewer manually resolves the blocked source.
Update the document analysis subagent to catch the access error and return an empty findings list as a successful result so the workflow completes without interruption.

explanation: "A core principle of error propagation in multi-agent systems is that, for routine, recoverable partial failures, the coordinator should propagate structured failure status, preserve the successful subagents' work, and continue when a useful final output can still be produced. In this scenario, one inaccessible source out of four is exactly such a failure: the correct pattern is to proceed with partial results and have the synthesis stage annotate coverage gaps, telling the user which findings are well supported and which topic areas could not be covered. This preserves the completed work of every other subagent and produces an honest, still-useful report instead of a total failure. (Some failures genuinely can invalidate an entire task, but a single blocked source in an otherwise successful research run is not one of them.)

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.The team wraps documentation generation in a headless script that runs claude -p with –allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob,Write" and a permission mode that auto-denies anything not pre-approved. A security review requires that these unattended runs can never execute shell commands. Run logs show that Claude still periodically emits Bash tool calls, which are auto-denied, wasting turns and cluttering the output before the run completes. Which change most reliably enforces the no-shell-commands constraint?

choices.text: Narrow the allowedTools list further so that it contains only the Read and Write tools for the run.
Append a system prompt instruction stating that shell commands must never be used during these runs.
Pass a bare disallowedTools rule for Bash so the tool definition is removed from Claude's context.
Switch the script to run in plan mode so the session is restricted to read-only tool execution.

explanation: "The core distinction here is between auto-approval and availability. The allowedTools option does not define the universe of tools Claude can see; it only pre-approves matching calls so they run without a permission prompt. Every other tool, including Bash, remains in Claude's context, and the model can still attempt to call it. In a headless run with a deny-by-default permission mode, those attempts are simply rejected, which is why the logs show wasted turns rather than a security breach; but the model keeps reasoning about a tool it can never use.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.A completed research run produced a fully cited report that the report-generation stage wrote to a local file, and the run's session ID was captured from the result message. Before anyone saved a copy, a scheduled cleanup job deleted the working directory, including the report file. The team wants to recover the report without re-running the web searches and document analysis. Which approach correctly reflects how Agent SDK session persistence works?

choices.text: Resume the session using the stored session ID and let the SDK restore the working directory to its state at the end of the run, including the deleted report file.
Resume the session using the stored session ID and prompt the agent to regenerate the report file from its retained conversation history.
Fork the session from the stored session ID so the new session recreates the original run's file artifacts alongside a copy of its history.
Start a fresh session and re-run the full research pipeline, since a session transcript can no longer be resumed once files in its working directory have changed.

explanation: "In the Claude Agent SDK, a session is the accumulated conversation: the prompt, every tool call, every tool result, and every response. The SDK writes this transcript to disk automatically (locally under ~/.claude/projects//*.jsonl) so a run can be resumed or forked later. Crucially, this is conversation persistence, not filesystem persistence: the SDK does not snapshot the working directory, and resuming a session never restores files. The documented mechanism for reverting file changes is file checkpointing, a separate feature with a different purpose.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.To keep the root CLAUDE.md lean, a teammate moved the team's container build standards (base image policies, multi-stage build requirements) into docs/container-standards.md and added an @docs/container-standards.md reference in the root CLAUDE.md, expecting the standards to load only when Claude works with Dockerfiles or docker-compose files. Session logs show the full standards appear in context on every run, including boilerplate generation tasks that never touch container files. Dockerfiles and compose files exist in every service directory across the repository. Which change achieves conditional loading of these standards?

choices.text: Repackage the standards as a skill in .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md whose description mentions Dockerfiles and compose files.

Skills are designed for on-demand, task-specific procedures that load when invoked or judged relevant, not conventions that must reliably accompany every edit to a given file type. Claude might not activate the skill when modifying a Dockerfile as part of a broader task, so the standards could be silently skipped.
Move the standards into a Markdown file under .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter whose paths field lists globs such as /Dockerfile and /docker-compose*.yml.

Replace the root-level reference with an @docs/container-standards.md reference in a directory-level CLAUDE.md inside each service directory. E Add YAML frontmatter with a paths field to docs/container-standards.md while keeping the @docs/container-standards.md reference in the root CLAUDE.md.

explanation: "Claude Code offers two distinct ways to modularize configuration, and they solve different problems. The @path import syntax in CLAUDE.md (for example @docs/container-standards.md) is an organizational tool: it lets you split a large memory file into smaller pieces, but every imported file is expanded into context at launch, exactly as if its text were pasted inline. Imports never make content conditional, which is why the container standards appeared in every session.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.In this system, a verification subagent runs after the report generator to check that each citation in the draft actually supports the claim it is attached to. Its prompt instructs it to "flag any citations that seem questionable." An audit shows that roughly 70% of its flags target accurate paraphrases or citations that correctly summarize a source without quoting it verbatim. Analysts have started dismissing all flags without checking, and a genuinely fabricated statistic recently made it into a published report. Which prompt change would most effectively reduce false flags while preserving detection of unsupported citations?

choices.text: Add an instruction telling the verifier to be conservative and raise a flag only for citations it is highly confident are genuinely unsupported by the source.
Require the verifier to emit its flags through a tool_use schema with enum severity values so every flag conforms to a strict, validated structure.
Instruct the verifier to flag a citation only when the source does not contain the claimed statement or statistic, and to quote the passage it checked.
Have the verifier attach a self-reported confidence score to each flag and configure the pipeline to suppress any flags scoring below a fixed threshold.

explanation: "The failure pattern here is the classic cost of vague criteria: the word 'questionable' has no testable definition, so the verifier applies a different interpretation on every run and flags things (accurate paraphrases, faithful summaries) that no analyst considers problems. Once a review signal is mostly noise, humans stop reading it, and precision failures in one area destroy trust in the signal everywhere, which is exactly how the fabricated statistic slipped through.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.An engineer asks the agent to audit three unrelated parts of an unfamiliar codebase in one request: the REST API handlers, the database migration scripts, and the CI shell scripts, with a findings summary for each area. The three audits share no dependencies, and each one requires dozens of Grep and Read calls whose raw output the engineer never needs to see. How should you decompose this task?

choices.text: Chain the three areas as a pipeline in which each subagent receives the previous subagent's full findings as input context before beginning its own audit.
Have the coordinator emit three Task tool calls in a single response, spawning one subagent per area to work in its own isolated context, then synthesize the three returned summaries.
Spawn one subagent per area across three separate turns, waiting for each subagent to finish and return its summary before starting the next one.
Have the main agent perform all three audits itself using Grep and Read in a single session, organizing the final report into one section per area.

explanation: "The decisive property in this scenario is independence: the three audits share no data dependencies, so nothing forces them to run in order. When subtasks are independent, the coordinator can spawn multiple subagents simultaneously by emitting several Task tool calls in a single response, and the whole job finishes in roughly the time of the slowest subtask instead of the sum of all of them.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.An engineer on this team used plan mode to have Claude Code design a refactor of the payment authorization module. The proposed plan looks correct, but because this code is security-sensitive, the team lead requires the engineer to review and approve each individual edit as Claude makes it during implementation. What should the engineer do at the plan approval prompt?

choices.text: Stay in plan mode and instruct Claude in the chat to implement the plan while asking before each file change.
Approve the plan with auto-accept edits enabled and review the completed changes afterward with git diff.
Approve the plan and choose the option that keeps manual review, so each edit prompts for explicit approval.
Reject the plan, press Shift+Tab to switch to accept edits mode, and paste the plan text back as a new prompt.

explanation: "Plan mode is a permission mode, not just a prompting style: while it is active, Claude can read files and investigate, but it does not edit source files until the plan is approved. The value of this design shows up at the moment of approval, because approving a plan is also the moment you choose the permission behavior for the implementation phase. The approval prompt offers options such as approving with auto mode or auto-accept edits, approving while manually reviewing edits, or staying in plan mode to revise the plan further.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.To keep conventions for this system organized, a teammate created rule files in subdirectories that mirror the package layout: .claude/rules/search/scraping-etiquette.md holds web-scraping conventions and .claude/rules/report/citation-format.md holds citation formatting standards. Neither file has YAML frontmatter; the teammate expected each rule to apply only when Claude Code works on files in the matching package. Session logs show the citation formatting standards loading into context even during sessions that only touch the search agent's code. What change achieves the intended conditional loading?

choices.text: Replace the rules directory with @import references in the root CLAUDE.md so each convention file loads only when Claude works in the corresponding package.
Add claudeMdExcludes patterns in settings so each rule file is skipped unless the session starts inside the matching package directory.
Add YAML frontmatter with a paths field of glob patterns (for example, paths: ["agents/report/**"]) to each rule file so it applies only to matching files.
Move the rule files to the top level of .claude/rules/, because rules nested in subdirectories are loaded unconditionally while top-level rule files are scoped automatically.

explanation: "Claude Code discovers every Markdown file under .claude/rules/ recursively, so subdirectories like .claude/rules/search/ and .claude/rules/report/ are a legitimate way to organize a growing rule set. What the directory structure does not do is scope loading: whether a rule is conditional depends entirely on its YAML frontmatter. A rule with a paths field containing glob patterns (such as agents/report/ or brace-expanded forms like src//*.{ts,tsx}) applies only when Claude works with matching files. A rule without a paths field loads unconditionally at launch and applies everywhere, with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md, which is exactly the behavior the team observed.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.This team's monorepo has a root CLAUDE.md that has grown to roughly 700 lines, covering conventions for test files, Terraform modules, API handlers, and frontend components that are spread across many directories. Engineers report that codebase exploration sessions feel degraded, and they suspect the large instruction file is consuming a significant share of the context window at the start of every session, even when most of its conventions are irrelevant to the files being explored. Which restructuring most effectively reduces this persistent context consumption while keeping the conventions available when they are relevant?

choices.text: Add an instruction at the top of the root CLAUDE.md directing Claude to ignore any sections that do not apply to the files currently being explored.
Relocate the conventions into each engineer's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md memory file so they no longer occupy project context.
Split the conventions into separate topic files and reference them all with @path imports from the root CLAUDE.md.
Move the conventions into modular rule files under .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter globs so each rule loads only when Claude works with matching files.

explanation: "The core mental model here is that CLAUDE.md files are persistent context, not configuration: everything in them is loaded into the context window and consumes tokens before exploration even begins. Anthropic recommends keeping each memory file concise (roughly under 200 lines) and moving toward modular, scoped instructions as they grow. A 700-line root file loaded into every session is a direct tax on the context budget that large codebase exploration already strains, since file reads, grep output, and command results can consume tens of thousands of tokens on their own.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.An engineer on your team proposes an optimization: since the document analysis subagent's findings are consumed by the synthesis subagent, the analysis subagent should hand its results directly to the synthesis subagent instead of routing them through the coordinator, which the engineer argues adds unnecessary overhead. All subagents are defined programmatically via the SDK's agents parameter and are invoked by the coordinator through the Agent tool. How should you respond to this proposal?

choices.text: Migrate the pipeline to agent teams so the analysis and synthesis agents can message each other directly without a coordinator relaying results.
Have the analysis subagent spawn the synthesis subagent as a nested subagent, passing its complete findings in the nested delegation prompt.
Keep the coordinator as the hub: it receives the analysis result and passes the relevant findings in the synthesis subagent's delegation prompt.
Instruct the synthesis subagent in its prompt to reference the analysis subagent's earlier findings, since both subagents run within the same session.

explanation: "The coordinator-subagent pattern in the Claude Agent SDK is a hub-and-spoke architecture by design. Each subagent is a separate agent instance with an isolated context window: it starts fresh, receives only the delegation prompt the invoking agent writes, does its work, and returns its final message to whoever spawned it. There is no channel for one sibling subagent to hand context to another; the parent is the only integration point. This is not an accidental limitation, it is the mechanism that gives the pattern its value: intermediate tool calls and verbose exploration stay inside each subagent, and the coordinator sees only distilled results it can route, filter, and combine.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.An engineer on this team writes a PreToolUse hook that uses updatedInput to prepend the team's standard license header to newly generated TypeScript files. They register the hook with the matcher string "src/**/*.ts", intending to intercept only writes under the src directory. Logging shows the callback never executes, even though Claude regularly writes files matching that pattern. What change makes the hook fire as intended?

choices.text: Change the matcher to "Write|Edit" and have the callback inspect tool_input.file_path to decide whether the write targets the src directory.
Register the callback under PostToolUse instead, since file paths are only resolved and available for matching after the tool executes.
Anchor the matcher pattern with ^ and $ so the regular expression engine matches the entire file path rather than a substring.
Add an instruction to CLAUDE.md directing Claude to include the license header whenever it writes files under the src directory.

explanation: "The mental model to hold is that a hook matcher filters on the event's target, which for tool-related events like PreToolUse and PostToolUse is the tool name. A matcher like Write|Edit matches those exact tool names, * or an empty matcher matches everything, and strings containing other regex characters are evaluated as unanchored regular expressions against the tool name. A file glob such as src/**/*.ts is therefore compared against names like Write and Bash, never against a path, so the callback silently never runs.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The document analysis subagent in this system downloads lengthy source materials (multi-hour hearing transcripts saved as text files) into a local corpus directory for analysis. When the subagent issues a Read call on one of these transcripts, the result comes back with a PARTIAL view notice indicating the file was too large to return in full. The subagent must still analyze the complete document before passing findings to the synthesis subagent. What is the most appropriate way for the subagent to access the full contents?

choices.text: Raise the BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH environment variable so the tool can return the file's complete contents.
Use Grep in content output mode with a match-everything pattern so the full document text is returned as search results.
Issue successive Read calls with offset and limit parameters to page through the transcript in sequential chunks.
Run cat on the transcript through the Bash tool so the entire document is returned in a single call.

explanation: "The Read tool is the purpose-built mechanism for loading file contents, and it has explicit behavior for files too large to return in one call: the response includes a PARTIAL view notice along with guidance to use the offset and limit parameters. The correct pattern is to page through the document in sequential, bounded chunks, which keeps each read within the tool's limits while still giving the agent access to every line. This design exists because dumping an enormous file into a single response would consume a huge slice of the context window at once; paged reads let the agent control how much content enters context per step, which matters in a multi-agent system where the analysis subagent must leave room for its own reasoning and structured findings.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.This team keeps the coordinator and subagent source code in a GitHub repository and has configured anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 in automation mode (a prompt input is set) so Claude reviews every pull request that changes agent orchestration logic. Pull requests opened by engineers are reviewed as expected, but pull requests opened by the team's dependency-update bot are rejected before Claude ever starts, so those changes get no review. What should the team change so the bot's pull requests receive automated reviews?

choices.text: Switch the workflow to a scheduled trigger, since scheduled events bypass the write-access check.
Grant the bot account write access to the repository so it passes the action's permission gate.
Add the bot account to allowed_non_write_users and supply a github_token so the action accepts it.
List the bot account in the action's allowed_bots input so its pull request events can start Claude runs.

explanation: "The Claude Code GitHub Action gates every run before Claude starts, because in a shared repository the actor who triggers a workflow effectively controls what Claude does and what tokens it consumes. The action applies two distinct gates: for human users on issue and pull request events, the triggering user must have write access unless they are explicitly permitted through allowed_non_write_users (which also requires a supplied github_token); for bot actors, the run is rejected outright unless the bot is named in the allowed_bots input. These are separate mechanisms, and confusing them is the trap here: giving a bot write access or adding it to the human allowlist does not satisfy the bot gate.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team's /scaffold command, defined in a legacy .claude/commands/scaffold.md file, generates boilerplate for new services. Over time the file has grown to contain several lengthy code templates pasted inline plus a shell helper script that Claude is told to retype and run, and when the command is invoked all of this content is loaded into the conversation. You want the core instructions to stay small, the templates to be read only when a particular one is needed, and the helper script to be runnable without its contents being loaded as context. How should you restructure this?

choices.text: Keep the single .claude/commands/scaffold.md file and use @import statements to pull the templates and helper script in from separate modular markdown files stored in the repository.
Migrate it to a project skill at .claude/skills/scaffold/SKILL.md, move each template into a supporting file it references, and keep the helper script in the folder as an executable.
Split the workflow into several smaller slash commands in .claude/commands/, one per template, and have developers invoke them in sequence when scaffolding a new service.
Move the templates and helper script into the project-level CLAUDE.md so they are available in every conversation, and slim the command file down to just the invocation steps.

explanation: "Claude Code has merged custom commands into skills: a file at .claude/commands/scaffold.md and a folder at .claude/skills/scaffold/SKILL.md both create the same /scaffold command, and legacy command files keep working. The reason the docs recommend skills is structural. A command is a single markdown file, so everything it needs must live inline and is loaded wholesale when the command's content is brought into context. A skill is a directory: SKILL.md is a lean entry point, detailed material sits in supporting reference files that Claude reads only when it actually needs that depth, and scripts stored in the folder can be executed rather than pasted into context. This progressive-disclosure design is the tradeoff skills exist to make: only skill descriptions are held in context during a normal session, and the full SKILL.md plus any referenced files load on demand, keeping the context window free for the work itself.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.Your extraction pipeline processes a batch of 40 vendor invoices in a single long-running conversation because the model must reconcile extracted line items against earlier invoices in the same session. After each invoice is extracted, the system calls a lookup_vendor MCP tool to validate the vendor record; the tool returns 45 fields per vendor, though only five (vendor_id, legal_name, tax_id, payment_terms, status) are ever used for validation. By the 30th invoice, the context window is nearly full and extraction accuracy on later invoices degrades noticeably. What change would most effectively preserve context for the remainder of each batch?

choices.text: Summarize the entire conversation history after each invoice is completed to compress the accumulated tool results.
Filter each lookup_vendor tool result down to the five fields used for validation before it is added to the conversation context.
Add a system prompt instruction directing the model to disregard vendor fields that are not relevant to validation.
Apply prompt caching with cache_control to the system prompt and tool definitions so each turn consumes less of the context window.

explanation: "The mental model here is that Claude is stateless: every request carries the full conversation, and everything in it, including every tool result, competes for the same finite context window. Tool outputs are a common silent budget killer because they often return far more data than the task needs. A lookup returning 45 fields when only 5 are used means roughly 90 percent of that content is pure overhead, repeated for every one of the 40 invoices. The highest-leverage fix is to trim tool outputs at the application layer before they ever enter the messages array, so the tokens saved are available for the extracted line items and reconciliation state that later invoices actually depend on.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. To cut costs, the team wants to move a recurring overnight workload to the Message Batches API: re-analyzing an archive of previously collected source documents to refresh citation metadata in older reports. Today the document-analysis subagent handles each document interactively through an agentic loop: it calls fetch_document, a custom MCP tool served by the agent's local, in-process MCP server, so only the client-side agent runtime can execute it and return the tool_result; there is no server-side tool equivalent available for it in the Messages API. After the tool result is returned to the model, one or two follow-up calls complete the extraction. An engineer proposes submitting each document's analysis as one request in a batch. What design change is required to make this workload batch-compatible?

choices.text: Restructure each analysis into a self-contained request by fetching the document text before batch submission and embedding it in the prompt, removing the need for mid-request client-side tool execution.
Include the MCP tool definitions in each batch request and set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so the batch infrastructure invokes fetch_document and continues the conversation automatically.
Split the archive across several smaller batches so each finishes well within the 24-hour processing window, since the multi-call loop only breaks when a batch expires.
Keep the agentic loop but assign a unique custom_id to each tool-call turn so the batch results can be correlated back to the correct in-progress conversation.

explanation: "The right mental model for the Message Batches API is a collection of independent, fire-and-forget Messages requests. Each item runs to completion on its own. Batches do support most Messages features, including tool use and server tools that Anthropic executes within the request; the limitation here is specific to client-executed tools. When a tool is served by a local MCP server in the agent runtime, your code must run the tool and send a tool_result back to the model, and a batch request offers no opportunity for that mid-request exchange. This is why the interactive loop, where the model calls fetch_document, observes the result, and continues reasoning, cannot run inside a batch as-is. Given the stem's constraint that no server-side equivalent exists, the workable pattern is to do the tool work up front: fetch each document's text during preparation, embed it in the prompt, and submit self-contained single-shot extraction requests. That preserves the 50% batch discount for a latency-tolerant overnight workload without breaking the analysis.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution. Your team's repository has a dist/ build output directory listed in .gitignore. Developers report that when Claude Code runs Glob searches like **/*.ts during refactoring sessions, the results include generated files under dist/, yet Grep content searches never surface matches from those same files. The team wants file-name pattern searches to consistently exclude gitignored files, matching the behavior they see from content searches. What should you do?

choices.text: Make no configuration change, since Glob already respects .gitignore by default and the dist files must have been committed to the repository.
Add an instruction to the project CLAUDE.md directing Claude to manually exclude gitignored directories whenever it runs Glob searches.
Replace Glob-based file discovery with Bash commands that pipe find output through filters to skip the ignored directories.
Set the CLAUDE_CODE_GLOB_NO_IGNORE environment variable to false before launching Claude Code so Glob respects .gitignore.

explanation: "The two built-in search tools in Claude Code have asymmetric defaults around ignore files, and that asymmetry is exactly what this team is seeing. Grep, which is built on ripgrep, searches file contents and respects .gitignore by default, so generated files under dist/ never appear in its results. Glob, which matches file names and paths against patterns like **/*.ts, does not respect .gitignore by default; it returns any matching file on disk, sorted by modification time and capped at 100 results. Because build output is frequently the most recently modified content in a repository, gitignored artifacts can even crowd out real source files in Glob results.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your platform team rolled out Claude Code with a restrictive custom permission configuration that prompts for confirmation on every Bash command and file edit, including harmless operations like running the test suite and formatting code, so developers have started reflexively approving everything. Last week a developer blanket-approved a Bash command that force-pushed over a teammate's branch, losing several commits. You need to redesign the approval policy so developers stay engaged for the decisions that actually matter. Which approach best achieves this?

choices.text: Have Claude Code report a self-assessed confidence score with each proposed action and prompt for approval only when the score falls below a threshold.
Classify actions by reversibility and impact, auto-approving reversible low-impact operations and requiring approval for irreversible high-impact ones.
Run every session in plan mode so developers review all proposed actions as part of an upfront plan before any execution of commands begins.
Require explicit developer approval for every Bash command the agent proposes while auto-approving all other tool calls without any review prompt.

explanation: "Effective human-in-the-loop design classifies agent actions along two independent axes: reversibility and impact. Routine operations like running the test suite or formatting code are low impact and reversible, so they should be auto-approved; a git push –force or a production deployment is high impact and irreversible, so it should require explicit, deliberate human approval. The mental model is that human attention is a scarce resource: if every action interrupts the developer, approval becomes a rubber stamp and the review step provides no real safety. Calibrating the escalation threshold to the consequences of each action keeps developers engaged precisely on the decisions where their judgment adds value.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.The synthesis subagent in this system is prompted to "flag any conflicting information between sources so the final report can note disagreements." Recent reports contain dozens of conflict annotations, but most flag two statistics drawn from different years or one source using a rounded figure. Analysts now skip the conflicts section entirely, and a genuine contradiction between two studies went unnoticed in a published report. Which prompt change to the synthesis subagent would most effectively reduce these false conflicts?

choices.text: Instruct the synthesis agent to be more conservative and flag only significant, high-confidence conflicts that would materially change the report's conclusions.
Cap the number of conflict annotations allowed per report at a small fixed limit so that only the most prominent source disagreements are surfaced to analysts.
Have the synthesis agent attach a self-reported confidence score to each conflict annotation and filter out any annotation below a fixed threshold before the report is generated.
Define explicit criteria flagging a conflict only when sources report incompatible values for the same metric, time period, and population, backed by quotes and publication dates.

explanation: "This failure follows a well-known pattern in precision-oriented prompting: an instruction like 'flag any conflicting information' is a subjective criterion, so the model must decide for itself what counts as a conflict, and it decides differently in every run. The observable symptom, analysts ignoring the entire conflicts section, is the classic cost of high false positive rates: once a category is noisy, humans stop trusting all findings in it, and real contradictions slip through.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.An engineer on this team is using Claude Code to explore the extraction pipeline's monorepo before adding support for a new document type. The investigation requires grepping across hundreds of schema definition files and reading several generated validation fixtures, each thousands of lines long. Midway through the session, the raw file contents and search output have filled most of the context window, and the agent's answers about the validation flow are becoming vague and inconsistent. The engineer still has several distinct investigation questions to answer (locating all schema registration points, tracing the validation error handling path, and listing downstream consumers). What is the most effective way to structure the remaining exploration?

choices.text: Run /clear before each remaining investigation question and have the agent re-read the relevant schema files from scratch for every single question.
Raise the auto-compact window with /autocompact so that compaction triggers later and the session can accumulate more exploration output before summarizing.
Delegate each remaining investigation question to a subagent that runs its searches and file reads in its own context and returns a concise summary.
Paste the full contents of the key validation fixtures into the project's CLAUDE.md file so the details persist in context for the rest of the exploration.

explanation: "In extended codebase exploration, the context window is the primary resource to manage: file reads, grep output, and command results all accumulate alongside the conversation, and performance degrades as it fills. Reading generated fixtures thousands of lines long is a classic way to burn tens of thousands of tokens on content whose relevance is mostly transient.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Midway through an accept edits session where an engineer has been rapidly iterating on small code changes, the engineer's next request is different: restructuring the module's caching layer, which has architectural implications and several valid approaches. The engineer wants Claude to propose an approach for review before any files change for this one task, then return to the fast iteration workflow. What is the most efficient way to accomplish this?

choices.text: Stay in accept edits mode and instruct Claude in the chat message to describe its plan first and not modify any files until told to proceed.
Prefix the caching request with /plan so plan mode applies to that prompt, then approve the resulting plan when it looks right.
Set permissions.defaultMode to plan in the project's .claude/settings.json so the review requirement is enforced for this task.
End the current session and restart Claude Code with claude --permission-mode plan to handle the caching work.

explanation: "Plan mode is a permission mode, one of the settings that determine what Claude Code may do without asking, rather than something Claude can be talked into honoring. In plan mode, Claude reads files and investigates but does not edit source files until you approve its proposed plan. That property makes it the right tool whenever a task has architectural implications or multiple valid approaches: you get the exploration and a reviewable proposal before anything touches disk.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.To catch semantic extraction errors that pass schema validation (values placed in the wrong fields, line items that do not sum to the stated total), this team added a second Claude instance as a reviewer. To give the reviewer full context, each review request includes the source document, the extracted JSON, and the complete reasoning transcript from the extraction call explaining why each value was chosen. Production audits show the reviewer approves nearly every extraction, including several with field misplacements that are obvious when the JSON is compared directly against the source document. Which change would most effectively improve the reviewer's error detection?

choices.text: Send the reviewer only the source document and the extracted JSON, excluding the extraction call's reasoning transcript from the review request.
Move the review into the extraction conversation itself so the same instance re-checks its output while the source document is still in context.
Enable extended thinking on the reviewer so it can reason more thoroughly over the extraction call's reasoning transcript before approving.
Tighten the extraction tool's input_schema by marking additional fields as required so schema validation surfaces the misplaced values.

explanation: "The value of an independent review instance comes precisely from what it does not see. When the reviewer receives the generator's full reasoning transcript, it inherits the same framing, assumptions, and justifications that produced the errors, so its most likely behavior is to rationalize the existing output rather than re-derive it. This is functionally the same failure mode as self-review, where a model that retains its generation context rarely questions its own decisions. The fix is architectural: give the reviewer only the ground truth (the source document) and the artifact under review (the extracted JSON), and let it perform a fresh comparison with no knowledge of how the answer was reached.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team's documentation automation script calls the Messages API with JSON outputs (output_config.format) to extract structured summaries of source files for the internal docs site. The validation-retry loop treats every HTTP 200 response as parseable JSON and, when parsing fails, resends the request with the parse error appended. Occasionally the loop cycles repeatedly on the same file: each response returns HTTP 200 and bills output tokens, but the content is a short prose message declining the task, and the response's stop_reason is "refusal". Which change most effectively fixes this validation-retry loop?

choices.text: Define an extraction tool with strict: true and force it with tool_choice so every response is guaranteed to conform to the extraction schema.
Check stop_reason before parsing, and route responses with a refusal stop reason to a separate handling path instead of resending the parse error.
Add exponential backoff between retries, treating the malformed responses as transient service errors that will succeed on a later attempt.
Raise max_tokens on each retry attempt so the model has enough room to finish emitting the complete JSON object before hitting the output limit.

explanation: "A robust validation-retry loop must distinguish why an output failed before deciding how to react, and the first signal to check is stop_reason. Every successful Messages API response includes one, and applications are expected to inspect it to decide whether to use the response, retry, or fall back. The mental model is a branch, not a single retry rule: end_turn responses are candidates for schema validation and self-correction retries; max_tokens means the output was truncated and the fix is a larger token budget; a refusal means the model declined the request, the API still returns HTTP 200 and bills the generated tokens, and the output may not match the schema at all.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.In this system, the synthesis subagent is given a scoped verify_fact tool so it can check individual claims without routing through the coordinator. Its description currently reads: "Verifies a factual claim against trusted sources." Trace logs show the synthesis subagent invokes verify_fact 40 to 60 times per report, re-verifying claims that already arrive with full citations in the findings passed from the search and analysis subagents, tripling report latency and token spend. What is the highest-leverage change to fix this behavior?

choices.text: Expand the verify_fact description to state it applies only to claims that lack a source and not to claims that already carry citations.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks further verify_fact invocations once a fixed per-report call budget has been exhausted.
Add several few-shot examples to the synthesis subagent's system prompt demonstrating turns where verify_fact was and was not called.
Remove verify_fact from the synthesis subagent's tool list and route all verification requests through the coordinator agent.

explanation: "Claude selects and invokes tools primarily based on their descriptions, which Anthropic documents as the single most important factor in tool performance. A strong description covers what the tool does, when to use it and when not to use it, what each parameter means, and caveats or limitations; the guidance is to aim for at least 3 to 4 sentences per tool. A one-line description like 'Verifies a factual claim against trusted sources' defines a capability but no boundary, so an agent optimizing for report accuracy will rationally verify every claim it touches, including ones that already arrived with citations from upstream subagents.

stem: SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow using custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md configuration, and to know when to use plan mode rather than direct execution.Your team's /plan-refactor slash command drives a helper script that calls the Messages API with a propose_refactor tool. The tool definition includes top-level "strict": true, and every response is a tool call whose input parses as valid JSON and conforms to the input_schema. However, in some runs the files_to_modify array in the tool call's arguments lists file paths that do not exist in the repository, and the downstream automation that stages those files for editing fails. Which change most effectively addresses this failure mode?

choices.text: Replace the tool-based approach with an assistant prefill that starts the response with an opening brace to force raw JSON output.
Tighten the input_schema by adding a regex pattern for the path fields and a description stating that every listed path must exist in the repository.
Set tool_choice to force the propose_refactor tool on every request so the model cannot respond with anything except a call to that tool.
Have the script validate the proposed file paths against the repository and, when invalid paths are found, resend the request with the specific validation error so Claude can correct the plan.

explanation: "This scenario hinges on the distinction between syntactic validity and semantic correctness. Strict tool use (top-level strict: true on a tool definition) constrains sampling so the tool call's input conforms to the input_schema and the tool name is valid. That guarantees well-formed, schema-conformant arguments, but a JSON Schema can only express constraints about shape, types, patterns, and allowed values. It has no visibility into external state such as which files actually exist in a repository, so a plan can be perfectly schema-valid while referencing paths that were never there.

stem: SCENARIO: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.A platform team uses Claude Code for developer productivity and packages their legacy-system exploration procedure as a project skill at .claude/skills/explore-legacy/SKILL.md. The skill instructs Claude to read source files, grep for patterns, and produce an architecture summary of a legacy module.
